response:
<advice>You are probably not failing because you are uniquely broken or boring. You are more likely making a few common calibration mistakes: reading friendliness as emerging friendship, pursuing after reciprocity has dropped, and measuring closeness through signs like photos or being included everywhere.</advice>
  <advice>The first change is this: stop treating time spent together as proof that a friendship should form. Walking after class every week and eating once means “we got along in that setting.” It does not yet mean “we are now real friends.” Friendship is not earned by evidence; it is built when both people keep choosing each other after there is no structural reason to.</advice>
  <advice>The second change is to use reciprocity much more strictly. If you invite, text, or follow up once and they do not match your energy, back off. Do not keep trying to convert a fading connection into a deeper one. The right read on silence is usually not “what did I do wrong,” but “this person is not choosing more closeness.” That is disappointing, but it is useful information.</advice>
  <advice>Stop using selfies, group photos, and Facebook as your scoreboard. Those are terrible indicators. Some close friends barely post each other; some people post constantly with people they are not close to at all. If you keep using social media as proof of your rank in people’s lives, you will become more bitter and less relaxed around them.</advice>
  <advice>Also drop the idea that going to nearly every event should move you from “orbiter” to “friend.” Attendance creates familiarity, not intimacy. Closeness usually comes from smaller interactions where people exchange something real: helping each other, sharing specific interests, remembering details, inviting one another into routines, and following through over time.</advice>
  <advice>So change your strategy from “show up everywhere” to “build a few mutual one-on-one or small-group threads.” Examples:
    <item>Invite one person to something specific and easy: coffee before class, lunch after a meeting, a walk to the library, working on a problem set together.</item>
    <item>Talk less about trying to become friends and more about shared activity and shared interest.</item>
    <item>Reveal a little more of yourself gradually—opinions, hobbies, stories, preferences—so people have something to attach to besides your presence.</item>
    <item>Notice who asks you questions back, follows up, remembers things, or initiates occasionally. Invest there.</item>
    <item>If someone never initiates, never follows up, or gives short polite responses, downgrade that connection without resentment.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Your studying-alone habit may be costing you more than you think. You do not have to give it up entirely, but if you always skip the more collaborative or recurring spaces, you may be missing the exact kind of repeated low-pressure contact that turns acquaintances into actual friends. Try joining some study sessions occasionally, or create another recurring activity that fits you better.</advice>
  <advice>With the girl from class specifically, the answer is simple: let that one go. Your initial outreach was fine. If she did not continue it, do not push. The lesson is not “women are impossible to befriend” or “I always get rejected.” The lesson is just that this was a context friendship that did not continue outside the context.</advice>
  <advice>Finally, watch your internal framing. If you think in terms like “ostracized,” “orbiter,” and “what did I do wrong” every time closeness does not develop, you will start approaching people from hunger and grievance. That tends to make interactions feel heavier. Instead think: “Some acquaintances will stay acquaintances. My job is to notice mutuality and build where it exists.” That mindset is much more attractive and much more accurate.</advice>
  <advice>If you want a practical rule: initiate once or twice, then look for matching effort. Build around shared routines. Prefer a few repeated smaller interactions over mass attendance. Ignore social media as evidence. And when interest is not mutual, exit cleanly instead of trying harder.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You are probably not failing because you are uniquely broken or boring. You are more likely making a few common calibration mistakes: reading friendliness as emerging friendship, pursuing after reciprocity has dropped, and measuring closeness through signs like photos or being included everywhere.</advice>
  <advice>The first change is this: stop treating time spent together as proof that a friendship should form. Walking after class every week and eating once means “we got along in that setting.” It does not yet mean “we are now real friends.” Friendship is not earned by evidence; it is built when both people keep choosing each other after there is no structural reason to.</advice>
  <advice>The second change is to use reciprocity much more strictly. If you invite, text, or follow up once and they do not match your energy, back off. Do not keep trying to convert a fading connection into a deeper one. The right read on silence is usually not “what did I do wrong,” but “this person is not choosing more closeness.” That is disappointing, but it is useful information.</advice>
  <advice>Stop using selfies, group photos, and Facebook as your scoreboard. Those are terrible indicators. Some close friends barely post each other; some people post constantly with people they are not close to at all. If you keep using social media as proof of your rank in people’s lives, you will become more bitter and less relaxed around them.</advice>
  <advice>Also drop the idea that going to nearly every event should move you from “orbiter” to “friend.” Attendance creates familiarity, not intimacy. Closeness usually comes from smaller interactions where people exchange something real: helping each other, sharing specific interests, remembering details, inviting one another into routines, and following through over time.</advice>
  <advice>So change your strategy from “show up everywhere” to “build a few mutual one-on-one or small-group threads.” Examples:
    <item>Invite one person to something specific and easy: coffee before class, lunch after a meeting, a walk to the library, working on a problem set together.</item>
    <item>Talk less about trying to become friends and more about shared activity and shared interest.</item>
    <item>Reveal a little more of yourself gradually—opinions, hobbies, stories, preferences—so people have something to attach to besides your presence.</item>
    <item>Notice who asks you questions back, follows up, remembers things, or initiates occasionally. Invest there.</item>
    <item>If someone never initiates, never follows up, or gives short polite responses, downgrade that connection without resentment.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Your studying-alone habit may be costing you more than you think. You do not have to give it up entirely, but if you always skip the more collaborative or recurring spaces, you may be missing the exact kind of repeated low-pressure contact that turns acquaintances into actual friends. Try joining some study sessions occasionally, or create another recurring activity that fits you better.</advice>
  <advice>With the girl from class specifically, the answer is simple: let that one go. Your initial outreach was fine. If she did not continue it, do not push. The lesson is not “women are impossible to befriend” or “I always get rejected.” The lesson is just that this was a context friendship that did not continue outside the context.</advice>
  <advice>Finally, watch your internal framing. If you think in terms like “ostracized,” “orbiter,” and “what did I do wrong” every time closeness does not develop, you will start approaching people from hunger and grievance. That tends to make interactions feel heavier. Instead think: “Some acquaintances will stay acquaintances. My job is to notice mutuality and build where it exists.” That mindset is much more attractive and much more accurate.</advice>
  <advice>If you want a practical rule: initiate once or twice, then look for matching effort. Build around shared routines. Prefer a few repeated smaller interactions over mass attendance. Ignore social media as evidence. And when interest is not mutual, exit cleanly instead of trying harder.</advice>
</response>

response:
Stop aiming to “hide emotions successfully.” Aim to look steady while staying honest with yourself. In practice, composure works better than suppression.

Use these instead:

<point>Prepare your body first. Nervousness shows on the face because the body is activated. Before the meeting, exhale longer than you inhale for 1–2 minutes, relax your jaw, unclench your tongue from the roof of your mouth, and drop your shoulders. A calmer body produces a calmer face.</point>

<point>Use a neutral resting expression, not a fake one. Keep your forehead relaxed, eyes soft, jaw loose, lips gently together or with a slight natural smile. Trying to “look confident” too hard often looks more unnatural than simply looking calm.</point>

<point>Slow down your pace. When people are nervous, they rush speech, blink more, and tighten facial muscles. Deliberately speak about 10–15% slower and pause before answering. That reads as thoughtful and composed.</point>

<point>Ground attention outward. If you monitor your face constantly, you’ll become more self-conscious. Put attention on the other person’s words, the question being asked, or one concrete object in the room. Outward focus reduces visible tension better than self-policing.</point>

<point>Rehearse the exact situation. Practice interview answers or social openings out loud, preferably on video. Don’t train yourself to erase emotion; train yourself to stay functional while a little nervous. Repetition makes your expression more natural.</point>

<point>If you blush, don’t fight it aggressively. Trying not to blush often makes blushing worse. Cool the body beforehand, avoid excess caffeine, breathe slowly, and let the sensation pass. A brief blush is usually less damaging than the effort to conceal it.</point>

<point>Use simple truthful framing when needed. In an interview or meeting, a calm “I’m a little nervous, but I’m glad to be here” can come across better than obvious overcontrol. Mild visible nerves are often interpreted as sincerity, not weakness.</point>

<point>Prioritize sleep, hydration, and stimulant control before high-stakes events. Lack of sleep and caffeine can amplify shakiness, facial tension, and blushing.</point>

A practical formula:
<step>1. Before the event: breathe out slowly, relax jaw/shoulders, review first 2–3 lines you want to say.</step>
<step>2. During the event: keep attention on the conversation, not your face.</step>
<step>3. If nerves show: pause, breathe, continue normally instead of trying to erase them.</step>

If this happens often enough that you feel driven to conceal yourself, work on anxiety management rather than facial masking alone. That might mean exposure practice, interview coaching, or talking with a therapist about social anxiety or blushing. The most reliable “trick” is not hiding better; it’s becoming less overwhelmed.

<point>Use a neutral resting expression, not a fake one. Keep your forehead relaxed, eyes soft, jaw loose, lips gently together or with a slight natural smile. Trying to “look confident” too hard often looks more unnatural than simply looking calm.</point>

<point>Slow down your pace. When people are nervous, they rush speech, blink more, and tighten facial muscles. Deliberately speak about 10–15% slower and pause before answering. That reads as thoughtful and composed.</point>

<point>Ground attention outward. If you monitor your face constantly, you’ll become more self-conscious. Put attention on the other person’s words, the question being asked, or one concrete object in the room. Outward focus reduces visible tension better than self-policing.</point>

<advice>You should treat this as a serious relationship problem, not a small rough patch. A partner who repeatedly insults you and the things you care about is not treating you well. Love by itself is not enough reason to stay.</advice>
  <advice>Focus on his current pattern, not who he was in the first three months. The affectionate beginning does not cancel out months of meanness, insults, and withdrawal.</advice>
  <advice>If you want clarity before ending it, have one direct conversation: tell him specifically that the insults, contempt for your interests, and lack of care are unacceptable, and that this relationship cannot continue if that is how he treats you. Do not argue about whether you are “too sensitive.” Stay with observable behavior.</advice>
  <advice>Then judge him by actions, not promises. If he minimizes it, blames you, laughs it off, or improves briefly and then returns to the same behavior, that is strong evidence you should leave.</advice>
  <advice>If you do not want to have that conversation, you do not need permission. You can end a relationship simply because being with him now makes you sad and he is consistently unkind.</advice>
  <advice>Tell a trusted friend or family member what has been happening and lean on them for support while you decide or if you break up. If you feel uneasy about his reaction, end it in a public place, by phone, or with support nearby.</advice>
  <advice>A healthy relationship should not require you to absorb insults to keep it. Choose the version of reality you are living in now, not the one you hope will come back.</advice>

<advice>
    <point>Do not break up over this before having one direct conversation.</point>
    <point>Your real issue is probably not "she spent less money." It sounds more like: "I gave a big, thoughtful gift, and when I opened mine I felt unknown, low-priority, or like there wasn’t much effort." That is the conversation to have.</point>
    <point>Be careful not to present this as a price complaint. If you go in saying "I spent 600 and you spent 100," the discussion will turn into money and scorekeeping. Focus on the feeling and mismatch instead: "I felt hurt because the gifts didn’t feel personal to me, and I realized we may have very different expectations around gift-giving."</point>
    <point>Also own your part clearly. You told her you wanted money and anime movies. That makes it harder to claim she ignored you. And giving an iPad may have set a standard she did not know she was being compared against. Say that out loud: "I think I may have created an expectation gap by giving a big gift while asking for simple things."</point>
    <point>Ask questions before making conclusions:
      <subpoint>What was her budget?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Did she think practical gifts were what you wanted?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Was she stressed, short on money, or trying to be useful rather than sentimental?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Does she usually show care in other ways outside gift-giving?</subpoint>
    </point>
    <point>If this is a one-off bad Christmas, treat it like a communication problem. If it fits a larger pattern—little effort, little thought, you feeling consistently unseen—then the gifts may just be the thing that exposed a deeper issue.</point>
    <point>A simple way to say it: "I want to be honest. I felt disappointed and hurt opening my gifts, not because I needed expensive stuff, but because it didn’t feel very personal to me. I realize I may not have given the clearest guidance either, and I don’t want to make this about money. I just want us to understand each other better."</point>
    <point>Then judge her more by her response than by the socks. If she listens, cares, and wants to understand, that is workable. If she gets dismissive and shows a repeated lack of effort across the relationship, that is more meaningful evidence than one holiday haul.</point>
    <point>So: don’t leave because of Christmas gifts alone. Talk first, drop the scorecard, figure out whether this was a mismatch or a pattern, and decide based on that.</point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You should assume you do not get to keep it.</advice>
  <advice>Stop treating the payments as yours. Do not spend them if you can avoid it. Move the money into a separate account if possible so you can repay it when asked.</advice>
  <advice>Notify the company in writing right away—payroll, HR, or finance—that you were terminated in January but are still receiving weekly wage payments. Keep copies of your message and any responses.</advice>
  <advice>Do not try to hide the mistake or structure things around “keeping” the money. If they discover it later, they may demand repayment, offset tax documents, send it to collections, or involve lawyers depending on the amount and your location.</advice>
  <advice>Ask them to confirm in writing:
    <item>the total overpaid amount,</item>
    <item>whether they will stop future payments immediately,</item>
    <item>how repayment should be made, and</item>
    <item>how they will correct payroll and tax reporting.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Be careful with taxes. If they issued pay slips, withholding, or year-end tax forms for money that was not actually owed, those records may need correction. If the amount is significant, consult an employment lawyer or accountant in your jurisdiction.</advice>
  <advice>If your real question is whether there is some legal exception that lets you keep mistaken wage payments, that depends heavily on local law and very specific facts, but in the ordinary case the answer is no.</advice>

response:
<advice>You probably cannot “ensure” you’ll be okay doing 80 hours a week on that schedule for a year. What you can do is treat it as a high-risk plan, set strict limits, and be ready to stop or modify it early.</advice>
  <advice>The biggest issue is sleep. If your day starts before 7 and your evening job ends around 11, you may only have a narrow window for commuting, eating, showering, winding down, and sleeping. If you cannot consistently get roughly 7 hours of sleep, this plan is not sustainable. That is the first test, not your motivation.</advice>
  <advice>Before starting, do the math for a real weekday: wake-up time, commute to job 1, commute to job 2, getting home, eating, hygiene, laundry, errands. If that leaves you chronically short on sleep, do not pretend discipline will fix it.</advice>
  <advice>Do not commit mentally to 12 months up front. Commit to a short trial, like 2 to 4 weeks, then reassess honestly. After that, reassess monthly. A plan that works for 10 days can still fail by week 6.</advice>
  <advice>Set hard stop conditions now. For example: if you are falling asleep driving, missing shifts, living on caffeine and junk food, getting sick repeatedly, feeling emotionally numb or angry all the time, or averaging too little sleep, you reduce hours or quit one job. Decide this before you are exhausted.</advice>
  <advice>Protect the basics aggressively:
    <item>Sleep: non-negotiable, same bedtime routine, dark room, phone away.</item>
    <item>Food: meal prep on days off; bring easy, high-protein, decent-calorie meals so you are not living on fast food.</item>
    <item>Hydration: keep water with you.</item>
    <item>Caffeine: use it carefully, not all day, and not late enough to wreck sleep.</item>
    <item>Movement: even 10–20 minutes of walking or stretching daily helps more than doing nothing.</item>
    <item>One real day off if possible, or at least one protected block every week with no work tasks.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Because you said you do not have much of a social life, build at least a minimal support/check-in system on purpose. That can be one family member, one friend, or one person you text weekly with a simple honest status update: sleep, stress, mood, whether you are still functioning. Isolation makes overwork worse.</advice>
  <advice>Also think about safety, not just toughness. Back-to-back shifts can make driving dangerous. If you ever catch yourself nodding off, drifting, or forgetting chunks of the drive, that is a serious warning sign.</advice>
  <advice>Financially, pressure-test the goal. Buying a house in cash is a huge target at 19, even in a cheaper area. Make sure you have run real numbers: take-home pay after taxes, actual monthly expenses, emergency fund, moving costs, closing costs, repairs, furnishings, insurance, and the possibility that one or both jobs change. If the math only works under perfect conditions, the plan is too brittle.</advice>
  <advice>A better version of this plan may be: work one full-time job plus a part-time second job, or work two jobs temporarily but with fewer total hours, or do the full schedule only for a shorter burst with a specific savings target. The goal is not to prove you can suffer; it is to reach the goal without wrecking your health or job performance.</advice>
  <advice>If you go forward, tell yourself this plainly: quitting or scaling back is not failure if the schedule is harming you. It is course correction.</advice>
  <advice>Your first month should answer one question only: are you actually sleeping enough, staying reliable at both jobs, and remaining physically and mentally steady? If the answer is no, change the plan early.</advice>

  <advice>You probably cannot “ensure” you’ll be okay doing 80 hours a week on that schedule for a year. What you can do is treat it as a high-risk plan, set strict limits, and be ready to stop or modify it early.</advice>
  <advice>The biggest issue is sleep. If your day starts before 7 and your evening job ends around 11, you may only have a narrow window for commuting, eating, showering, winding down, and sleeping. If you cannot consistently get roughly 7 hours of sleep, this plan is not sustainable. That is the first test, not your motivation.</advice>
  <advice>Before starting, do the math for a real weekday: wake-up time, commute to job 1, commute to job 2, getting home, eating, hygiene, laundry, errands. If that leaves you chronically short on sleep, do not pretend discipline will fix it.</advice>
  <advice>Do not commit mentally to 12 months up front. Commit to a short trial, like 2 to 4 weeks, then reassess honestly. After that, reassess monthly. A plan that works for 10 days can still fail by week 6.</advice>
  <advice>Set hard stop conditions now. For example: if you are falling asleep driving, missing shifts, living on caffeine and junk food, getting sick repeatedly, feeling emotionally numb or angry all the time, or averaging too little sleep, you reduce hours or quit one job. Decide this before you are exhausted.</advice>
  <advice>Protect the basics aggressively:
    <item>Sleep: non-negotiable, same bedtime routine, dark room, phone away.</item>
    <item>Food: meal prep on days off; bring easy, high-protein, decent-calorie meals so you are not living on fast food.</item>
    <item>Hydration: keep water with you.</item>
    <item>Caffeine: use it carefully, not all day, and not late enough to wreck sleep.</item>
    <item>Movement: even 10–20 minutes of walking or stretching daily helps more than doing nothing.</item>
    <item>One real day off if possible, or at least one protected block every week with no work tasks.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Because you said you do not have much of a social life, build at least a minimal support/check-in system on purpose. That can be one family member, one friend, or one person you text weekly with a simple honest status update: sleep, stress, mood, whether you are still functioning. Isolation makes overwork worse.</advice>
  <advice>Also think about safety, not just toughness. Back-to-back shifts can make driving dangerous. If you ever catch yourself nodding off, drifting, or forgetting chunks of the drive, that is a serious warning sign.</advice>
  <advice>Financially, pressure-test the goal. Buying a house in cash is a huge target at 19, even in a cheaper area. Make sure you have run real numbers: take-home pay after taxes, actual monthly expenses, emergency fund, moving costs, closing costs, repairs, furnishings, insurance, and the possibility that one or both jobs change. If the math only works under perfect conditions, the plan is too brittle.</advice>
  <advice>A better version of this plan may be: work one full-time job plus a part-time second job, or work two jobs temporarily but with fewer total hours, or do the full schedule only for a shorter burst with a specific savings target. The goal is not to prove you can suffer; it is to reach the goal without wrecking your health or job performance.</advice>
  <advice>If you go forward, tell yourself this plainly: quitting or scaling back is not failure if the schedule is harming you. It is course correction.</advice>
  <advice>Your first month should answer one question only: are you actually sleeping enough, staying reliable at both jobs, and remaining physically and mentally steady? If the answer is no, change the plan early.</advice>
</response>

response:
Small talk gets easier when you stop treating it like “being interesting” and start treating it like “making the next exchange easy.”

Focus on 4 basic skills:

<skill>1. Notice and comment on what is already happening.</skill>
This is the easiest way to start.
Examples:
- “How do you know the host?”
- “Have you taken this class before?”
- “This line is moving so slowly.”
- “That presentation was a lot—what did you think?”

You do not need a brilliant opener. You need something simple and relevant.

<skill>2. Ask questions that are easy to answer, then follow up once.</skill>
Bad small talk often dies because people ask either:
- questions that are too broad: “So, what’s up?”
- or too interview-like: one question after another with no reaction

Try this pattern:
- Ask
- Listen
- React
- Follow up

Example:
- “What do you do?”
- “I’m in marketing.”
- “Oh, nice—what kind?”
- “Mostly social media for nonprofits.”
- “That sounds interesting. Is it more creative or more analytics-heavy?”

The follow-up matters more than the first question.

<skill>3. Share a little about yourself too.</skill>
If you only ask questions, it can feel like an interview. After they answer, add a small piece of yourself.
Example:
- “I just started there a few months ago.”
- “I haven’t been here before either.”
- “I always overthink these networking events.”

Short self-disclosure helps the other person feel like they’re talking with you, not being examined by you.

<skill>4. End topics cleanly instead of panicking when energy drops.</skill>
A conversation does not have to flow endlessly. You can shift naturally:
- “That makes sense. So how do you know everyone here?”
- “Speaking of work, how’s your semester going?”
- “I should grab a drink, but it was nice talking to you.”

A lot of people think they’re bad at conversation when really they’re bad at transitions.

Use this simple formula:
<formula>Observation or context + open question + follow-up + small self-share</formula>

Examples:
- “This class seems intense. What made you sign up for it?”
- “You mentioned you’re new here—how are you liking it so far?”
- “I’ve heard that team is busy all the time. Has that been true for you?”

A few practical rules:
- Ask about what is present: place, event, role, food, class, work, shared annoyance, shared task.
- Prefer open questions, but keep them specific.
- Listen for topics with energy: hobbies, recent changes, opinions, funny inconveniences, plans.
- Don’t aim for perfect chemistry with everyone.
- Don’t force deep conversation with people who clearly prefer direct, minimal interaction.

What to avoid:
- Rapid-fire questioning
- Overexplaining
- Turning every reply back to yourself
- Panicking during pauses
- Thinking every conversation has to become meaningful

Practice on purpose in low-stakes settings:
- cashier or barista
- coworker before a meeting
- classmate before class starts
- neighbor in passing

Set tiny goals:
- start one conversation a day
- ask one follow-up question
- share one small detail about yourself
- stay in the interaction 30 seconds longer than usual

If you often freeze, memorize a few reusable questions:
- “How’s your week going?”
- “What’s been keeping you busy lately?”
- “How do you know everyone here?”
- “What did you think of that?”
- “Have you done this before?”

If your problem is anxiety rather than lack of skill, the fix is repetition, not finding the perfect line. Most people do not remember awkward moments nearly as much as you do.

A good target is not “be charismatic.” It’s:
<target>be curious, be easy to talk to, and keep the ball moving.</target>

If you want, I can also give you:
- a 10-minute daily practice plan
- a cheat sheet of small-talk questions
- or examples for work, dating, and group settings

response: You generally do not need to correct them. In most ordinary social situations, the better etiquette is what you’re doing now: let them tell it, respond politely, and if you want, ask a slightly different question or react to a different part of the story. A good rule is: - If the repetition is harmless and brief, let it pass. - If correcting them would mainly save a little time but risk embarrassing them, don’t correct them. - If you’re very close, in private, and brevity actually matters, you can mention it gently. If you do want to signal that you remember it, do it in a way that joins them rather than shuts them down. For example: - “Oh right, this was the one where…” - “Yes, I remember this part—what happened after that again?” - “I think you told me a bit of this before, but remind me…” Those work better than “You already told me that,” which can sound like a rebuke. It also depends on the context: - Casual conversation: usually just listen. - Group setting: avoid calling them out; public correction is more embarrassing. - Close friend who prefers directness: a light, warm acknowledgment can be fine. - If repetition is frequent and seems linked to memory issues: prioritize kindness and don’t make their memory the focus. So the basic etiquette is: preserve dignity first, correct only when there’s a real reason, and if you do mention it, do it gently and collaboratively.

judge_raw: Interrupting someone to say they already told you the story is the strongest concrete concern. Multiple stakeholders note this can feel dismissive or embarrassing, especially in front of others. If the speaker has memory difficulties or cognitive decline, pointing out the repetition directly can cause shame, anxiety, or make them self-conscious about their memory. Cutting them off can make the whole interaction awkward for other people present, not just the speaker. Letting them finish and listening politely is strongly supported. It avoids putting them on the spot and keeps the interaction comfortable. Asking new questions is a substantive positive because it keeps the exchange engaged and kind rather than merely tolerating repetition. Your newer approach is especially considerate in casual social settings where preserving the other person’s dignity matters more than correcting the repetition. You generally do not need to correct them. In most ordinary social situations, the better etiquette is what you’re doing now: let them tell it, respond politely, and if you want, ask a slightly different question or react to a different part of the story. A good rule is: - If the repetition is harmless and brief, let it pass. - If correcting them would mainly save a little time but risk embarrassing them, don’t correct them. - If you’re very close, in private, and brevity actually matters, you can mention it gently. If you do want to signal that you remember it, do it in a way that joins them rather than shuts them down. For example: - “Oh right, this was the one where…” - “Yes, I remember this part—what happened after that again?” - “I think you told me a bit of this before, but remind me…” Those work better than “You already told me that,” which can sound like a rebuke. It also depends on the context: - Casual conversation: usually just listen. - Group setting: avoid calling them out; public correction is more embarrassing. - Close friend who prefers directness: a light, warm acknowledgment can be fine. - If repetition is frequent and seems linked to memory issues: prioritize kindness and don’t make their memory the focus. So the basic etiquette is: preserve dignity first, correct only when there’s a real reason, and if you do mention it, do it gently and collaboratively.

response:
<advice>You are not being too sensitive. The central issue is not whether his preferences are valid; it is that he is responding to your boundaries by pressuring, criticizing, and shaming you.</advice>
  <advice>Wanting lingerie, more sex, or a different lifestyle does not entitle him to punish you when you are uncomfortable or say no. “Ignoring my needs” is not an appropriate response to “I don’t want to” or “I don’t feel well.” In a healthy relationship, a no to sex or sexual clothing is accepted without anger, guilt, or retaliation.</advice>
  <advice>The body comments are especially concerning. A partner who makes constant remarks about you being unfit or unhealthy, while knowing or being able to see that this hits your self-esteem, is not giving constructive feedback. He is wearing you down.</advice>
  <advice>Step back and ask a more useful question than “am I too defensive?” Ask: “Do I feel safe saying no to him?” and “Do I feel respected after honest conversations?” From what you wrote, the answer appears to be no.</advice>
  <advice>You should set this out plainly if you want to test whether the relationship can continue: “When I say no to sex or lingerie, I need that to be respected without anger, guilt, or insults. Comments about my body and health are not acceptable. If we have compatibility issues, we discuss them respectfully, not by blaming me.”</advice>
  <advice>Then watch his behavior, not just his words. If he minimizes this, argues that you owe him these things, keeps criticizing your body, or repeats the same pattern, treat that as your answer. This may simply be incompatibility, but the way he is handling it is unhealthy enough that ending the relationship would be reasonable.</advice>
  <advice>It would also help to reality-check with people you trust or a therapist, especially because your self-esteem has already been affected and you mentioned a history of food restriction. Protecting your mental health here is important.</advice>
  <advice>You do not need to become more sexually accommodating, less cautious, or more ashamed of your body to earn basic respect.</advice>

response:
<advice>The way to help her is not to help her get over her ex faster. It is to respect that she is not ready.</advice>
  <advice>If you really care for her, stop thinking in terms of speeding up her healing. You cannot make that process faster in a healthy way, and trying will likely make her feel pressured, watched, or responsible for your feelings.</advice>
  <advice>Do this instead:</advice>
  <steps>
    <step>Take her words literally. She said to give her time, so give her time.</step>
    <step>Do not position yourself as the solution to her breakup pain. That often creates rebound dynamics and pressure.</step>
    <step>If you stay in contact, keep it low-pressure and normal. No repeated check-ins about whether she is over him yet, no emotional pushing, no “I’ll wait forever” speeches, no trying to prove you are better than her ex.</step>
    <step>If you want clarity, say something simple once: “I like you, but I respect that you need time. I’m not going to pressure you. If and when you feel ready, you can let me know.” Then let your actions match that.</step>
    <step>Focus on being a respectful person, not a savior. Support means making room for her feelings, not managing them toward the outcome you want.</step>
    <step>Protect yourself too. Don’t put your life on hold indefinitely or build your identity around “doing anything for her.” That mindset can become unhealthy for both of you.</step>
  </steps>
  <advice>Also prepare for the possibility that “give me time” may not end in a relationship with you. Respecting her means accepting that her healing process belongs to her, and the result may be uncertainty, a long delay, or a no.</advice>
  <advice>If you cannot be around her without quietly waiting, hoping, and pushing for signs, create more distance. That is more respectful than staying close while trying to steer her toward you.</advice>
  <advice>In short: don’t try to move her on from her ex. Respect her pace, remove pressure, and let her choose if and when she is ready.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>The way to help her is not to help her get over her ex faster. It is to respect that she is not ready.</advice>
  <advice>If you really care for her, stop thinking in terms of speeding up her healing. You cannot make that process faster in a healthy way, and trying will likely make her feel pressured, watched, or responsible for your feelings.</advice>
  <advice>Do this instead:</advice>
  <steps>
    <step>Take her words literally. She said to give her time, so give her time.</step>
    <step>Do not position yourself as the solution to her breakup pain. That often creates rebound dynamics and pressure.</step>
    <step>If you stay in contact, keep it low-pressure and normal. No repeated check-ins about whether she is over him yet, no emotional pushing, no “I’ll wait forever” speeches, no trying to prove you are better than her ex.</step>
    <step>If you want clarity, say something simple once: “I like you, but I respect that you need time. I’m not going to pressure you. If and when you feel ready, you can let me know.” Then let your actions match that.</step>
    <step>Focus on being a respectful person, not a savior. Support means making room for her feelings, not managing them toward the outcome you want.</step>
    <step>Protect yourself too. Don’t put your life on hold indefinitely or build your identity around “doing anything for her.” That mindset can become unhealthy for both of you.</step>
  </steps>
  <advice>Also prepare for the possibility that “give me time” may not end in a relationship with you. Respecting her means accepting that her healing process belongs to her, and the result may be uncertainty, a long delay, or a no.</advice>
  <advice>If you cannot be around her without quietly waiting, hoping, and pushing for signs, create more distance. That is more respectful than staying close while trying to steer her toward you.</advice>
  <advice>In short: don’t try to move her on from her ex. Respect her pace, remove pressure, and let her choose if and when she is ready.</advice>
</response>

response:
You need to stop treating this as a hinting problem and treat it as a compatibility-and-boundaries problem.

Do not bring it up during sex next time. Bring it up fully, outside the bedroom, in plain language. Say something like:

“I don’t want sex that starts with you telling me to suck you off or you trying to put it in right away. I need kissing, touching, and foreplay that actually turns me on. Rubbing my boobs for a second or trying to finger me immediately does not do it for me. I’m not okay with sex being focused on getting you off while I’m left unsatisfied. If we keep having sex, it needs to change.”

Be specific. Tell him:
- what actually turns you on
- what you do not want as the automatic opening move
- what pace you need
- what you want him to do for your pleasure
- what you will stop doing if he ignores that

For example:
- “Don’t tell me to suck it the second we start.”
- “I want kissing and slow buildup first.”
- “If I’m not turned on yet, do not try to just stick it in.”
- “Oral for you is not something I’m doing every time as the default.”
- “If sex becomes one-sided again, I’m stopping.”

Then follow through. If he says “suck it,” say “No, not like that.” If he tries to skip to penetration, stop him physically and verbally: “No. I’m not ready, and I already told you what I need.” If he gets annoyed, plays games, sulks, or acts like you’re ruining things, that is information.

Pay attention less to whether he says the right words afterward and more to whether he changes his behavior consistently. The biggest issue here is not that he is unskilled. It is that you already raised this, he joked, ignored it shortly after, and then got mad when you objected again. That pattern suggests he is not just clueless; he is also not taking your sexual experience seriously.

You also need to stop consenting to sex you already expect to resent. Being “in the mood” is not the same as agreeing to the same unsatisfying routine. If he starts the usual script, stop participating. Otherwise you keep teaching both him and yourself that your needs come second.

And yes, sex can be a deal breaker. Not because orgasm is the only thing that matters, but because mutual care, responsiveness, and respect matter. If after a direct conversation he still treats sex like access to your body for his satisfaction, then the problem is bigger than technique. It is about whether he cares enough to adjust when you say something is not working for you.

So your next step is:
1. Have one clear, direct, non-hint conversation outside of sex.
2. State specific wants and boundaries.
3. Stop going along with the old pattern.
4. Watch what he does, not what he promises.
5. If he keeps dismissing, deflecting, or centering himself, end the sexual relationship—and possibly the whole relationship.

You do not need to keep having sex that leaves you irritated, resentful, and unheard.

“I don’t want sex that starts with you telling me to suck you off or you trying to put it in right away. I need kissing, touching, and foreplay that actually turns me on. If we keep having sex, it needs to change.”

Be specific. Tell him:
- what actually turns you on
- what you do not want as the automatic opening move
- what pace you need
- what you want him to do for your pleasure
- what you will stop doing if he ignores that

For example:
- “Don’t tell me to suck it the second we start.”
- “I want kissing and slow buildup first.”
- “If I’m not turned on yet, do not try to just stick it in.”
- “Oral for you is not something I’m doing every time as the default.”
- “If sex becomes one-sided again, I’m stopping.”

Pay attention less to whether he says the right words afterward and more to whether he changes his behavior consistently. The biggest issue here is not that he is unskilled. If after a direct conversation he still treats sex like access to your body for his satisfaction, then the problem is bigger than technique. It is about whether he cares enough to adjust when you say something is not working for you.

So your next step is:
1. Have one clear, direct, non-hint conversation outside of sex.
2. State specific wants and boundaries.
3. Stop going along with the old pattern.
4. Watch what he does, not what he promises.
5. If he keeps dismissing, deflecting, or centering himself, end the sexual relationship—and possibly the whole relationship.

You do not need to keep having sex that leaves you irritated, resentful, and unheard.</response>

response:
<advice>You should not fake being married at work for the next couple of years.</advice>
  <advice>The practical answer is: unwind the lie early, simply, and with as little extra detail as possible. Every week you wait makes it harder and riskier.</advice>
  <advice>The cleanest option is to tell the hiring manager, privately, before you start or very soon after starting: that you answered inaccurately in the interview when asked about your marital status, you got flustered, and you want to correct the record now. Do not add more story. Do not justify it by saying you thought it helped you. Do not invent a breakup, separation, or dead spouse.</advice>
  <advice>A simple version is enough: “I want to correct something from the interview. When I was asked about my marital status, I answered inaccurately. I was flustered and should have said I prefer to keep personal matters private. I’m correcting that now because I don’t want any misunderstanding going forward.”</advice>
  <advice>If you are unwilling to say outright that you lied, the next-best damage-control option is still to stop feeding the story immediately. Do not buy a ring. Do not create photos, a fake social media presence, or a fake spouse persona. Do not bring a date to spouse events to play the role. Do not tell additional coworkers more details. The lie gets exponentially worse once props and third parties are involved.</advice>
  <advice>If the topic comes up socially, pivot to privacy and brevity: “I keep my personal life pretty separate from work.” That is far safer than continuing the fiction.</advice>
  <advice>You should also recognize a separate issue: asking whether you are married in an interview is often inappropriate and may be unlawful depending on location. But that is not a shield for your lie, and you should not try to weaponize that fact while also maintaining the deception.</advice>
  <advice>Your real choices are:
    <option>Correct it now and accept some embarrassment.</option>
    <option>Keep lying, increase the risk, and eventually face a larger trust problem.</option>
  </advice>
  <advice>The first option is far better. Short-term awkwardness is much cheaper than a long-running fraud about a basic personal fact.</advice>

  <advice>A simple version is enough: “I want to correct something from the interview. When I was asked about my marital status, I answered inaccurately. I was flustered and should have said I prefer to keep personal matters private. I’m correcting that now because I don’t want any misunderstanding going forward.”</advice>
  <advice>If you are unwilling to say outright that you lied, the next-best damage-control option is still to stop feeding the story immediately. Do not buy a ring. Do not create photos, a fake social media presence, or a fake spouse persona. Do not bring a date to spouse events to play the role. Do not tell additional coworkers more details. The lie gets exponentially worse once props and third parties are involved.</advice>
  <advice>If the topic comes up socially, pivot to privacy and brevity: “I keep my personal life pretty separate from work.” That is far safer than continuing the fiction.</advice>
  <advice>You should also recognize a separate issue: asking whether you are married in an interview is often inappropriate and may be unlawful depending on location. But that is not a shield for your lie, and you should not try to weaponize that fact while also maintaining the deception.</advice>
  <advice>Your real choices are:
    <option>Correct it now and accept some embarrassment.</option>
    <option>Keep lying, increase the risk, and eventually face a larger trust problem.</option>
  </advice>
  <advice>The first option is far better. Short-term awkwardness is much cheaper than a long-running fraud about a basic personal fact.</advice>

<advice>Do not try to mess with them further. Stop contacting the line, stop logging into the account, and do not change anything else.</advice>
  <advice>Your next steps should be procedural:
    <step>Preserve evidence: keep the emails, screenshots, timestamps, the phone number, account number if visible, and notes of exactly what you changed and when.</step>
    <step>Contact the carrier’s fraud department directly, not general chat if possible. Tell them your email was used without permission, that you used password recovery, changed the password and PIN, and sent one message to the line. Ask them to document the incident, remove your email from the account, secure the account through their fraud process, and tell you whether they want you to restore access or leave it untouched.</step>
    <step>Secure your email account: change your email password, enable MFA, review forwarding rules, login history, recovery addresses, and any signs your mailbox was compromised.</step>
    <step>If the carrier indicates identity theft or stolen-payment fraud, file reports through the appropriate official channels they recommend. If you are in the U.S., that may include IdentityTheft.gov and possibly a police report if needed for documentation.</step>
    <step>If you receive more messages or charges tied to this, add them to your record and forward them to the fraud team rather than engaging with the user.</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you already changed the credentials, be upfront about that when you report it. Hiding it makes the situation worse. The safest course now is to disengage and let the carrier and, if necessary, law enforcement handle it.</advice>

    <step>Contact the carrier’s fraud department directly, not general chat if possible. response:
<advice>
    <point>Your problem is not just envy. It is that you appear to have surrendered authorship of your own life while also carrying resentment about the price you paid for the marriage’s current shape.</point>
    <point>Do not try to “overcome” these feelings by shaming yourself out of them. “I shouldn’t complain” is making things worse. Treat the feelings as information. They are telling you at least three things: you feel unseen, you feel overburdened, and you feel your own development has been deferred.</point>
    <point>Stop using the background-character frame as your private truth. It may describe how you feel, but if you keep repeating it internally, it will become your identity. Replace it with a more useful question: “Where have I stopped actively building a life that feels like mine?” That question gives you leverage; the old one mainly gives you pain.</point>
    <point>You need to separate two issues that are currently tangled together:</point>
    <point>First: unresolved resentment about his financial mistakes and their long tail.</point>
    <point>Second: your own lack of expansion, visibility, autonomy, or fulfillment.</point>
    <point>If you do not separate them, every one of his opportunities will feel like theft, even when they are legitimate work obligations.</point>
    <point>Have a direct conversation with him that is not framed as “you’re the main character and I’m nothing.” Make it behavioral and specific. For example: “I feel like my role has narrowed to responsibility and support, and I’m becoming resentful. I need us to look at division of labor, time for my own goals, and how we make decisions about money and opportunity.”</point>
    <point>Be prepared to name what “my own goals” actually are. If you cannot answer that yet, that is part of the issue. You likely need something that is yours and not merely adjacent to him: work growth, training, travel, creative work, friendships, a business idea, volunteering, education, or protected time that is treated as real, not optional.</point>
    <point>Make the invisible visible. Write down:</point>
    <point>- all recurring boring responsibilities you carry</point>
    <point>- all cognitive load you carry</point>
    <point>- what freedoms he has that you do not</point>
    <point>- what opportunities you want in the next 6 to 12 months</point>
    <point>This will help you move from mood to negotiation.</point>
    <point>On the financial issue, decide whether you are still in repair mode or stuck in blame mode. If there are still concrete consequences, create a shared financial recovery plan with dates, rules, and transparency. If you already have a plan and you are still reliving the injury, then the emotional wound needs direct attention, not just budgeting.</point>
    <point>Watch your language. Thinking “stupid mistakes” may feel honest, but if contempt enters the relationship, it will poison the conversation. You do not need to excuse the damage to speak about it in a way that leaves room for accountability and change.</point>
    <point>Also examine whether you have been passively waiting to be noticed rather than explicitly asking for room, support, and redistribution. That is common, but it does not work well. If you need more say, more time, more recognition, or less household burden, ask for those things concretely.</point>
    <point>If this is hard to untangle, couples therapy would likely help—not because the marriage is necessarily failing, but because your current story about the marriage is becoming corrosive. A good therapist can help you both distinguish practical imbalance from emotional narrative and help you renegotiate the structure of your life together.</point>
    <point>Your task is not to become more grateful for being sidelined. Your task is to reclaim a life that feels authored by you while addressing the resentment honestly and without contempt.</point>
  </advice>

judge_reasoning:
<concerns>
    <concern>Most serious: you initially encouraged her to go on hormonal birth control after she had already made clear she did not want it because of prior side effects. Even though you later dropped it, that earlier push is concrete and likely relevant to why she now seems to be framing this as something she should do for the relationship rather than something she wants for herself.</concern>
    <concern>Her stated reason is relationship anxiety, not contraceptive preference: she explicitly said she does not want the hormones, worries about lowered sex drive and weight gain, and is doing it partly to reduce the chance you might seek a preferred sexual experience elsewhere. That suggests insecurity and comparison to your past, not a freely enthusiastic medical choice.</concern>
    <concern>Your reply, “I’m not tempted I hope you are not,” shifted the focus from reassuring her insecurity to introducing suspicion about her. That is grounded in the text and could make her feel accused or less safe being vulnerable.</concern>
    <concern>You summarize this as “she is afraid I will cheat if she does not,” which misses part of what she actually said: she also linked it to what she believes feels better sexually and to comparisons with your past partners. Reducing it to cheating alone risks misunderstanding the real issue, which appears to be insecurity, comparison, and pressure around sexual compatibility.</concern>
    <concern>A lesser but still grounded issue: by discussing your sexual history and preferences in a way that she connected to “all the girls you used to” sleep with, you may have contributed to her feeling compared to prior partners and needing to compete.</concern>
  </concerns>
  <supports>

    <support>You did directly tell her that cheating is not something she should worry about, which is a meaningful reassurance given what she said.</support>
  </supports>
  <overall>On balance, the biggest issue is not that she suddenly wants birth control; it is that she appears willing to take a medication she expects to dislike because she feels insecure about meeting a sexual standard she associates with your past and your preferences. response:
<advice>You should make plans to leave this job, and you should do it in the cleanest way you can rather than trying to “push through” a role that is already harming you physically and mentally.</advice>
  <advice>The key point is not whether the company is good in the long run. The key point is that this specific job is a bad fit now. You asked for office work, disclosed that you could not do much heavy lifting, and then ended up in 13+ hour physically punishing warehouse shifts that are leaving you injured and depressed. That is enough information to stop treating this like a normal adjustment period.</advice>
  <advice>Do not keep going just to avoid disappointing your fiancé. His opinion matters, but it should not override the fact that you are being worn down this fast. If you stay only to protect his feelings or reputation, you are likely to burn out harder, quit in a worse way, or get hurt.</advice>
  <advice>That said, missing work for an interview was not a good move. Don’t repeat that. From here, handle the exit directly and professionally.</advice>
  <advice>Best course:</advice>
  <advice>
    <step>Tell your fiancé plainly, today, that this is no longer a question of “getting used to it.” Say that you are in pain, bruised, mentally unwell, and cannot safely continue much longer.</step>
    <step>If you can manage one final conversation at work, tell the manager in direct terms: the role is not physically sustainable for you, you disclosed that from the start, and you need to resign or need your last day to be immediately or very soon.</step>
    <step>If you can afford to give brief notice, do that. Even a short, professional resignation is better than disappearing. If you truly cannot safely do another shift, resign effective immediately.</step>
    <step>Do not argue about whether it is “fair” to the men in the warehouse. This is about job fit and safety, not asking for special treatment.</step>
    <step>If there is HR, you can notify them too, especially that you disclosed lifting limitations up front and the workload/hours are not manageable. Keep it factual.</step>
    <step>While waiting on the other job, focus on replacing income quickly and tightening expenses, because the financial reality does matter.</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you resign, keep the wording simple: this warehouse role is not a fit physically, you disclosed your limitations at hire, and you are resigning. Do not make it dramatic, and do not make your fiancé defend the decision for you.</advice>
  <advice>If your fiancé reacts as though the main issue is embarrassment at work, pay attention to that. A partner should care more that you are being hurt than that a manager might be inconvenienced.</advice>
  <advice>So: don’t stick it out longer just because others want you to. Exit professionally if you can, immediately if you must, and stop treating this as a test of toughness.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should make plans to leave this job, and you should do it in the cleanest way you can rather than trying to “push through” a role that is already harming you physically and mentally.</advice>
  <advice>The key point is not whether the company is good in the long run. The key point is that this specific job is a bad fit now. You asked for office work, disclosed that you could not do much heavy lifting, and then ended up in 13+ hour physically punishing warehouse shifts that are leaving you injured and depressed. That is enough information to stop treating this like a normal adjustment period.</advice>
  <advice>Do not keep going just to avoid disappointing your fiancé. His opinion matters, but it should not override the fact that you are being worn down this fast. If you stay only to protect his feelings or reputation, you are likely to burn out harder, quit in a worse way, or get hurt.</advice>
  <advice>That said, missing work for an interview was not a good move. Don’t repeat that. From here, handle the exit directly and professionally.</advice>
  <advice>Best course:</advice>
  <advice>
    <step>Tell your fiancé plainly, today, that this is no longer a question of “getting used to it.” Say that you are in pain, bruised, mentally unwell, and cannot safely continue much longer.</step>
    <step>If you can manage one final conversation at work, tell the manager in direct terms: the role is not physically sustainable for you, you disclosed that from the start, and you need to resign or need your last day to be immediately or very soon.</step>
    <step>If you can afford to give brief notice, do that. Even a short, professional resignation is better than disappearing. If you truly cannot safely do another shift, resign effective immediately.</step>
    <step>Do not argue about whether it is “fair” to the men in the warehouse. This is about job fit and safety, not asking for special treatment.</step>
    <step>If there is HR, you can notify them too, especially that you disclosed lifting limitations up front and the workload/hours are not manageable. Keep it factual.</step>
    <step>While waiting on the other job, focus on replacing income quickly and tightening expenses, because the financial reality does matter.</step>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you resign, keep the wording simple: this warehouse role is not a fit physically, you disclosed your limitations at hire, and you are resigning. Do not make it dramatic, and do not make your fiancé defend the decision for you.</advice>
  <advice>If your fiancé reacts as though the main issue is embarrassment at work, pay attention to that. A partner should care more that you are being hurt than that a manager might be inconvenienced.</advice>
  <advice>So: don’t stick it out longer just because others want you to. Exit professionally if you can, immediately if you must, and stop treating this as a test of toughness.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>You do not need to break up just because he is poor. You do need to stop financing this relationship.</advice>
  <advice>The immediate issue is not his income level. It is that you have been saying yes to expenses you cannot actually afford, and now you are resentful and short on money. So fix that part first, directly and clearly.</advice>
  <advice>Tell him something like: “I need to talk about money. I can’t keep paying for lunches, coffees, dates, or group obligations anymore. I’ve gone beyond what I can afford, and I need to stop. This isn’t me blaming you for not having money. I just have to stay within my own limit.”</advice>
  <advice>Also say the part you have not been saying: “If we go out and it costs money, I may not be able to cover both of us. So from now on, if you can’t afford something, we should skip it or do something free.”</advice>
  <advice>That conversation should happen before you decide on a breakup, because right now he may not fully understand that your “it’s on me” has turned into a real burden.</advice>
  <advice>Then change your behavior, not just your wording:</advice>
  <advice>- Stop paying for his daily lunch and coffee.</advice>
  <advice>- Stop offering to cover both of you unless you have consciously decided you can afford that specific expense.</advice>
  <advice>- Stop rescuing social situations like birthdays or group dinners that are too expensive.</advice>
  <advice>- Choose free or very cheap dates: walks, campus time, tea, studying together, simple snacks, visiting friends, festivals, public places, anything within budget.</advice>
  <advice>- Set a hard monthly cap for discretionary spending and do not exceed it.</advice>
  <advice>- Stop lying to your parents.</advice>
  <advice>If he responds with understanding and adapts, the relationship may be fine. If he becomes angry, guilt-trips you, keeps expecting you to pay, or acts as though your money is the only way the relationship can function, then breaking up would make sense—not because he is poor, but because the relationship would be financially unhealthy and disrespectful of your limits.</advice>
  <advice>You should also be honest with yourself about one thing: you are not only reacting to his poverty; you are reacting to a lifestyle mismatch. You want frequent paid outings, and he often cannot afford them. That does not make either of you wrong, but it may make the relationship difficult unless both of you can accept a much cheaper way of spending time together.</advice>
  <advice>So your next step is simple: have the money conversation now, set the boundary now, and watch what happens. Do not keep paying while you “think about it.”</advice>

    What you describe sounds like strong test anxiety, and the part about feeling like you might pass out matters. Focus on two tracks at once: what to do during a test, and what to set up before the next one.

    <during_test>
      <step>Slow your body down first. Try this discreetly: inhale through your nose for 4 seconds, exhale for 6 to 8 seconds, and repeat 5 times. A longer exhale helps reduce the physical panic response.</step>
      <step>Unclench your muscles on purpose: drop your shoulders, relax your jaw, loosen your hands, and place both feet on the floor.</step>
      <step>Orient yourself to the room. Silently name 3 things you see, 2 things you feel, and 1 thing you hear. This can help pull your mind out of the panic spiral.</step>
      <step>If your mind goes blank, do not fight the whole test at once. Find the easiest question and answer that first. Momentum helps thinking come back.</step>
      <step>If you start getting dizzy or feel close to fainting, raise your hand and tell the instructor you are feeling physically unwell. That is important.</step>
    </during_test>

    <before_test>
      <step>Practice the calming method before you need it. Do the same breathing exercise once or twice a day so it is familiar during an exam.</step>
      <step>Simulate the test conditions when studying: set a timer, sit upright, no phone, and do a few practice problems under mild pressure. This can make the real setting feel less shocking.</step>
      <step>Use a short reset statement when the fear starts, such as: “Anxiety is loud, but it is not a prediction,” or “I only need to do the next question.”</step>
      <step>Reduce avoidable physical triggers: sleep as well as you can, eat beforehand, hydrate, and be careful with too much caffeine if it makes you shakier.</step>
      <step>Arrive a little early so you are not starting the exam already activated by rushing.</step>
    </before_test>

    <get_support>
      <step>Tell your teacher or exam instructor exactly what happens: “During tests I get so anxious I feel faint and can’t think clearly.” Since you already raised the issue, keep going and be specific.</step>
      <step>Ask whether there are supports available, such as a quieter room, brief breaks, extra time, or access to school counseling or disability services if applicable.</step>
      <step>If this happens often, talk to a school counselor, doctor, or mental health professional. Feeling like you may pass out during exams is worth professional help, especially if it is recurring.</step>
    </get_support>

      For your next test, use this plan:
      <step>Before the test: 1 minute of slow exhale breathing.</step>
      <step>At the start: read all directions once, then begin with the easiest question.</step>
      <step>If panic rises: feet on floor, shoulders down, 5 slow breaths, then do only the next problem.</step>
      <step>If you feel faint: alert the instructor immediately.</step>
    </simple_plan>

  </advice>

response:
<advice>You need to decide between two honest positions: either you are willing to date her at her pace with no expectation that kissing or sex will happen on your schedule, or you are not compatible and should end the relationship kindly. What you should not do is stay while hoping she will speed up because you are graduating soon.</advice>
  <advice>Do not make this conversation about your masculinity, your self-confidence, or how she should "at least try" kissing. Those frames will sound like pressure, even if you do not mean them that way. Her boundaries are not a referendum on your worth, attractiveness, or manhood.</advice>
  <advice>Also drop the "sex before I graduate" idea entirely. Keep that as a private thought to challenge, not a goal to pursue with her. Based on what you described, that expectation is badly mismatched with her stated comfort level.</advice>
  <advice>If you talk to her, the point should be clarity, not persuasion. Ask about her experience of the relationship and her comfort, and be prepared to hear that she may not want physical affection anytime soon. A good version sounds like: "I want to check in about how you feel in this relationship and what pace feels comfortable to you. I do not want to pressure you. I also want to be honest that physical affection matters to me, so I am trying to understand whether we are compatible rather than asking you to change for me."</advice>
  <advice>Do not ask why she is not comfortable "with you" specifically, because that can turn her boundary into a personal indictment. A better question is: "What kinds of affection feel okay to you right now, if any?" and "Do you see yourself wanting more physical affection eventually, or do you not know?" That keeps the focus on her comfort rather than your insecurity.</advice>
  <advice>If her answer is that she does not know, is not ready, or may not want much physical affection for a long time, then believe her. Do not treat that as a challenge to overcome. Your choice then is simple: accept the relationship as it is, or end it respectfully because your needs and timelines do not match.</advice>
  <advice>If you end it, be honest without blaming her. Say something like: "I respect your boundaries, but I think we want different kinds of relationships and I do not want either of us to feel pressured or inadequate." Do not say she made you feel less like a man, and do not imply she failed some test by not kissing you.</advice>
  <advice>You should also examine whether you are looking for a partner or for practice before college. It is normal to want dating experience, but if that is a major driver, then you owe it to future partners to be more transparent with yourself and to choose relationships where your goals align better.</advice>
  <advice>In short: respect her pace fully, stop attaching your self-worth to her boundaries, abandon the graduation/sex timeline, and have one clear non-pressuring compatibility conversation. After that, either commit to the relationship as it actually is or let it go.</advice>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Do not start trying for a baby until this feels clearer to you. Not because dreams are prophetic, but because they are clearly activating something unresolved enough to affect your judgment and peace of mind.
    </point>
    <point>
      You do need to tell your husband more than “I’m hesitant.” The issue is not that you owe him every raw detail immediately; it is that this is a shared life decision, and he deserves an honest account of why you are pausing. If you hide the real reason entirely, you turn your private confusion into secrecy, and secrecy is more damaging than the dreams.
    </point>
    <point>
      You can tell him in a way that is honest without making it sound like you want your ex. For example: “I need to slow down on trying for a baby. I’ve been having recurring dreams about my ex, and I don’t think they mean I want him back, but they are stirring up unresolved feelings or old guilt that I don’t understand yet. I don’t want to become parents while I’m mentally preoccupied by something I haven’t sorted through. This is about me wanting clarity, not about wanting anyone else.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Be careful not to over-interpret the dreams themselves. Dreams are often symbolic, repetitive, and emotionally sticky without pointing to a literal desire. Given the content you described—apologizing, urgency, trying to speak to him—it may be less about romantic longing and more about unfinished emotional business, guilt, identity, nostalgia, or anxiety about life transitions. The timing matters: starting a family is a major threshold, and big thresholds often stir up old versions of ourselves and unresolved chapters.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not contact your ex to “get closure.” Based on what you wrote, that would be far more likely to create real problems than solve the internal one. Closure is usually something you build internally, not something another person reliably gives you years later.
    </point>
    <point>
      Bring this back to your therapist directly and more forcefully. Say plainly: “When I brought up these dreams and you said I have a vivid imagination, I felt dismissed. This is affecting whether I feel ready to start a family, so I need us to take it seriously and explore what it may represent.” A good therapist should be able to repair that moment and help you examine the meaning, even if the conclusion is still that dreams are not literal.
    </point>
    <point>
      If your therapist continues to brush it off after you say that clearly, consider a second opinion or a few sessions focused specifically on this issue. The standard is not whether she is generally helpful; it is whether she can engage a topic that is materially affecting your marriage and family planning.
    </point>
    <point>
      In the meantime, track the dreams. Write down what happens, what emotion is strongest in each dream, and what is happening in your life when they intensify. Pay particular attention to themes like regret, unfinished conversations, fear of making irreversible choices, grief over younger versions of yourself, or anxiety about losing freedom. Those patterns are often more revealing than the identity of the person in the dream.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your immediate job is not to decode your ex; it is to understand what your mind is doing with him. Once you know that, the decision about timing for a child will probably feel less clouded.
    </point>
  </advice>

The timing matters: starting a family is a major threshold, and big thresholds often stir up old versions of ourselves and unresolved chapters.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not contact your ex to “get closure.” Based on what you wrote, that would be far more likely to create real problems than solve the internal one. Closure is usually something you build internally, not something another person reliably gives you years later.
    </point>
    <point>
      Bring this back to your therapist directly and more forcefully. Say plainly: “When I brought up these dreams and you said I have a vivid imagination, I felt dismissed. This is affecting whether I feel ready to start a family, so I need us to take it seriously and explore what it may represent.” A good therapist should be able to repair that moment and help you examine the meaning, even if the conclusion is still that dreams are not literal.
    </point>
    <point>
      If your therapist continues to brush it off after you say that clearly, consider a second opinion or a few sessions focused specifically on this issue. The standard is not whether she is generally helpful; it is whether she can engage a topic that is materially affecting your marriage and family planning.
    </point>
    <point>
      In the meantime, track the dreams. Write down what happens, what emotion is strongest in each dream, and what is happening in your life when they intensify. Pay particular attention to themes like regret, unfinished conversations, fear of making irreversible choices, grief over younger versions of yourself, or anxiety about losing freedom. Those patterns are often more revealing than the identity of the person in the dream.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your immediate job is not to decode your ex; it is to understand what your mind is doing with him. Once you know that, the decision about timing for a child will probably feel less clouded.
    </point>
  </advice>

<step>3. Contact academic advising/dean of students/disability support.</step>
Ask specifically:
- what happens if you are failing multiple classes
- whether there are late withdrawals, incomplete options, medical exceptions, reduced course load options, or temporary accommodations
- what documentation counseling can provide if needed

Do not assume your only options are "push through" or "get kicked out."

<step>4. Stop aiming to fix the whole semester at once.</step>
For the next 48 hours, your only goals are:
- attend or contact counseling
- send the emails
- show up to the next class or, if you cannot, email before it starts
- complete one small piece of coursework, even 10-20 minutes worth

When anxiety is this high, motivation usually comes after action, not before it.

<step>5. Use an anti-avoidance rule for class.</step>
Your job is not "feel ready." Your job is:
- get dressed
- go to campus or open the class portal
- stay for 10 minutes minimum

If after 10 minutes you are still overwhelmed, you can reassess. But do not decide from bed or from panic. The hardest part is usually the approach.

<step>6. Make school tasks smaller than your brain thinks they should be.</step>
Examples:
- open assignment page
- write the title
- answer one question
- study for 5 minutes
- make one flashcard
- email one person

"Do homework" is too big. "Spend 8 minutes on problem 1" is doable.

<step>7. Reduce the shame loop.</step>
Right now the pattern is likely:
stress -> skip -> fall behind -> more shame -> more skipping.
Your immediate goal is not perfect performance. It is breaking that loop with visible actions, even tiny ones.

<step>8. If you are panicking before class or a test, use a short physical reset.</step>
Try:
- inhale 4, exhale 6, for 2 minutes
- cold water on hands or face
- name 5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear
- walk for 3 minutes before entering class

- 10 minutes: look up advising/dean of students
- 10 minutes: do one tiny assignment task
- then stop and reassess
