response:
<advice>You were not wrong to report repeated theft of food you were buying for students. The key moral fact here is simple: someone kept taking resources intended for kids after you tried clear, nonconfrontational ways to stop it. Reporting that was reasonable.</advice>
  <advice>You should also separate your choice from what happened next. You did not secretly install a camera. You did not fire anyone. Security and administration chose how to investigate and what employment action to take. Coworkers may be collapsing those steps together, but they are not the same.</advice>
  <advice>That said, your problem now is no longer “Was I allowed to report this?” It is “How do I function in a workplace where people are blaming me?” Handle that directly and professionally.</advice>
  <advice>Do not quit immediately unless there are broader problems that make the job untenable. A first-year teacher in a difficult school setting is already under strain, and leaving in the heat of a social backlash may hurt you more than help you.</advice>
  <advice>Instead, take these steps:</advice>
  <advice>1. Stop discussing the incident casually with coworkers. If anyone raises it, keep your response short: “I reported that student food I paid for was repeatedly disappearing after I tried to handle it informally. I wasn’t involved in the investigation decisions.” Then end the conversation.</advice>
  <advice>2. Document hostility if it becomes concrete: dates, who said what, whether it interfered with work, and whether it included gossip, exclusion, or retaliation. General coldness is hard to address; specific conduct is easier.</advice>
  <advice>3. Ask for a private meeting with your principal or direct supervisor. Focus on workplace fallout, not moral debate. Say that you need a professional environment, that gossip about a personnel matter is spreading, and that the hostility is affecting your work.</advice>
  <advice>4. Consider adjusting the snack system with administrative approval. Ask whether there is a school-supported way to provide snacks, a locked storage option, or access to counselor/social-worker resources, PTA support, grants, or a pantry program. You should not have to keep personally subsidizing this without structure.</advice>
  <advice>5. Build alliances with a few steady colleagues rather than trying to win over everyone. In a tense school culture, one or two sane, professional coworkers matter more than broad popularity.</advice>
  <advice>If you want, you can acknowledge one narrow point without admitting wrongdoing: “I’m sorry the situation ended badly for everyone.” That is different from saying, “I shouldn’t have reported theft.” Don’t apologize for protecting resources meant for students.</advice>
  <advice>The administrative assistant’s spreading of the story is especially inappropriate. If that person’s gossip is fueling the hostility, include that in your documentation and raise it with administration as unprofessional disclosure of a personnel-related matter.</advice>
  <advice>If, after you try these steps, the hostility remains severe or your administration refuses to support you, then reassess whether this school is a workable place to stay. But decide that based on the school’s response to ongoing unprofessional behavior, not because you think reporting the theft was itself wrong.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You were not wrong to report repeated theft of food you were buying for students. The key moral fact here is simple: someone kept taking resources intended for kids after you tried clear, nonconfrontational ways to stop it. Reporting that was reasonable.</advice>
  <advice>You should also separate your choice from what happened next. You did not secretly install a camera. You did not fire anyone. Security and administration chose how to investigate and what employment action to take. Coworkers may be collapsing those steps together, but they are not the same.</advice>
  <advice>That said, your problem now is no longer “Was I allowed to report this?” It is “How do I function in a workplace where people are blaming me?” Handle that directly and professionally.</advice>
  <advice>Do not quit immediately unless there are broader problems that make the job untenable. A first-year teacher in a difficult school setting is already under strain, and leaving in the heat of a social backlash may hurt you more than help you.</advice>
  <advice>Instead, take these steps:</advice>
  <advice>1. Stop discussing the incident casually with coworkers. If anyone raises it, keep your response short: “I reported that student food I paid for was repeatedly disappearing after I tried to handle it informally. I wasn’t involved in the investigation decisions.” Then end the conversation.</advice>
  <advice>2. Document hostility if it becomes concrete: dates, who said what, whether it interfered with work, and whether it included gossip, exclusion, or retaliation. General coldness is hard to address; specific conduct is easier.</advice>
  <advice>3. Ask for a private meeting with your principal or direct supervisor. Focus on workplace fallout, not moral debate. Say that you need a professional environment, that gossip about a personnel matter is spreading, and that the hostility is affecting your work.</advice>
  <advice>4. Consider adjusting the snack system with administrative approval. Ask whether there is a school-supported way to provide snacks, a locked storage option, or access to counselor/social-worker resources, PTA support, grants, or a pantry program. You should not have to keep personally subsidizing this without structure.</advice>
  <advice>5. Build alliances with a few steady colleagues rather than trying to win over everyone. In a tense school culture, one or two sane, professional coworkers matter more than broad popularity.</advice>
  <advice>If you want, you can acknowledge one narrow point without admitting wrongdoing: “I’m sorry the situation ended badly for everyone.” That is different from saying, “I shouldn’t have reported theft.” Don’t apologize for protecting resources meant for students.</advice>
  <advice>The administrative assistant’s spreading of the story is especially inappropriate. If that person’s gossip is fueling the hostility, include that in your documentation and raise it with administration as unprofessional disclosure of a personnel-related matter.</advice>
  <advice>If, after you try these steps, the hostility remains severe or your administration refuses to support you, then reassess whether this school is a workable place to stay. But decide that based on the school’s response to ongoing unprofessional behavior, not because you think reporting the theft was itself wrong.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Do not resign until the new job is fully locked in: written offer, compensation confirmed, start date confirmed, and any background/reference process either completed or clearly defined.
    </point>
    <point>
      Tell the new employer directly and professionally that you would prefer they not contact your current manager before an offer is finalized, because your search is confidential. That is normal. You do not need to accuse your boss of abuse; say something like: “My current employer is not aware of my search, so I’d appreciate if you could avoid contacting my current manager at this stage. I can provide prior supervisors, colleagues, or other professional references instead.”
    </point>
    <point>
      If they insist on a current-employer reference, try to redirect them to HR, payroll, or someone who can verify employment only. If this is a small company without HR, offer alternative references: former managers, senior coworkers, clients, vendors, or anyone credible who has seen your work.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not coach the new employer with a dramatic story unless they ask. Keep it simple, factual, and future-focused: you are moving to a role with better alignment, remote work, and stronger growth opportunities.
    </point>
    <point>
      Start documenting now. Save copies, where lawful and appropriate, of performance-related evidence you may need: campaigns you ran, metrics, examples of content, appointment volume influenced by your work, positive messages, calendars, and any written instructions showing your actual responsibilities. Do not take confidential patient data or proprietary material. The point is to preserve proof of your work in case a reference issue comes up.
    </point>
    <point>
      Assume your boss may react badly once you resign. Because of that, prepare for two possibilities: either they accept notice, or they terminate you immediately. Given your paycheck-to-paycheck situation, if you can afford it, build even a very small cushion before giving notice. If you cannot, then all the more reason to wait until the new position is certain.
    </point>
    <point>
      When it is time to resign, keep the resignation short. Example: “I’m resigning from my position effective [date]. Thank you for the opportunity. I will do my best to document my work and support a smooth transition through my final day.” Do not list grievances in the letter.
    </point>
    <point>
      Give notice only if it is safe and financially sensible. Two weeks or 15 days is courteous, but not morally required if there is a real chance of retaliation that could jeopardize your income or the new role. Your first duty is to protect your livelihood.
    </point>
    <point>
      During any notice period, become extremely procedural. Ask for priorities in writing where possible. Use neutral phrasing: “I have A, B, and C pending. Which should I do first?” That reduces opportunities for conflict and helps protect you if your boss later claims you ignored instructions.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not confront him about being rude, unfair, or abusive on the way out unless there is a formal HR channel and a clear benefit to doing so. In a small business with a volatile boss, that usually creates risk without helping you.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the new employer asks why they should discount a negative reference, answer calmly with specifics about structure, not character assassination: your role expanded far beyond marketing, decision-making was tightly centralized, and the fit was no longer sustainable. Then pivot to evidence of your work and other references.
    </point>
    <point>
      The ethical path here is not to manipulate the process; it is to manage it transparently and prudently. Ask for confidentiality, provide alternative references, give straightforward reasons for leaving, and exit professionally once your next job is secure.
    </point>
  </advice>
  <practical_script>
    “I’m excited about this opportunity. My current employer doesn’t know I’m searching, so I’d appreciate keeping my search confidential and not contacting my current manager at this stage. I’m happy to provide former supervisors and other professional references who can speak to my work.”
  </practical_script>
  <resignation_script>
    “Please accept this message as my resignation from my position, effective [date]. Thank you for the opportunity. Between now and my last day, I will document my current work and do what I can to support a smooth handoff.”
  </resignation_script>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Do not resign until the new job is fully locked in: written offer, compensation confirmed, start date confirmed, and any background/reference process either completed or clearly defined.
    </point>
    <point>
      Tell the new employer directly and professionally that you would prefer they not contact your current manager before an offer is finalized, because your search is confidential. That is normal. You do not need to accuse your boss of abuse; say something like: “My current employer is not aware of my search, so I’d appreciate if you could avoid contacting my current manager at this stage. I can provide prior supervisors, colleagues, or other professional references instead.”
    </point>
    <point>
      If they insist on a current-employer reference, try to redirect them to HR, payroll, or someone who can verify employment only. If this is a small company without HR, offer alternative references: former managers, senior coworkers, clients, vendors, or anyone credible who has seen your work.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not coach the new employer with a dramatic story unless they ask. Keep it simple, factual, and future-focused: you are moving to a role with better alignment, remote work, and stronger growth opportunities.
    </point>
    <point>
      Start documenting now. Save copies, where lawful and appropriate, of performance-related evidence you may need: campaigns you ran, metrics, examples of content, appointment volume influenced by your work, positive messages, calendars, and any written instructions showing your actual responsibilities. Do not take confidential patient data or proprietary material. The point is to preserve proof of your work in case a reference issue comes up.
    </point>
    <point>
      Assume your boss may react badly once you resign. Because of that, prepare for two possibilities: either they accept notice, or they terminate you immediately. Given your paycheck-to-paycheck situation, if you can afford it, build even a very small cushion before giving notice. If you cannot, then all the more reason to wait until the new position is certain.
    </point>
    <point>
      When it is time to resign, keep the resignation short. Example: “I’m resigning from my position effective [date]. Thank you for the opportunity. I will do my best to document my work and support a smooth transition through my final day.” Do not list grievances in the letter.
    </point>
    <point>
      Give notice only if it is safe and financially sensible. Two weeks or 15 days is courteous, but not morally required if there is a real chance of retaliation that could jeopardize your income or the new role. Your first duty is to protect your livelihood.
    </point>
    <point>
      During any notice period, become extremely procedural. Ask for priorities in writing where possible. Use neutral phrasing: “I have A, B, and C pending. Which should I do first?” That reduces opportunities for conflict and helps protect you if your boss later claims you ignored instructions.
    </point>
    <point>
      Do not confront him about being rude, unfair, or abusive on the way out unless there is a formal HR channel and a clear benefit to doing so. In a small business with a volatile boss, that usually creates risk without helping you.
    </point>
    <point>
      If the new employer asks why they should discount a negative reference, answer calmly with specifics about structure, not character assassination: your role expanded far beyond marketing, decision-making was tightly centralized, and the fit was no longer sustainable. Then pivot to evidence of your work and other references.
    </point>
    <point>
      The ethical path here is not to manipulate the process; it is to manage it transparently and prudently. Ask for confidentiality, provide alternative references, give straightforward reasons for leaving, and exit professionally once your next job is secure.
    </point>
  </advice>
  <practical_script>
    “I’m excited about this opportunity. My current employer doesn’t know I’m searching, so I’d appreciate keeping my search confidential and not contacting my current manager at this stage. I’m happy to provide former supervisors and other professional references who can speak to my work.”
  </practical_script>
  <resignation_script>
    “Please accept this message as my resignation from my position, effective [date]. Thank you for the opportunity. Between now and my last day, I will document my current work and do what I can to support a smooth handoff.”
  </resignation_script>
</response>

response:
Stop using bleach for this. It is not helping much with label removal, and it adds avoidable fumes and residue.

Use a simpler batch process:

<step>1. Empty and prep the bottles.</step>
<detail>Make sure there is no medication left inside. If there is, ask your pharmacy about a medication take-back option rather than throwing it away.</detail>

<step>2. Soak in hot water with dish soap.</step>
<detail>Fill a sink or tub with hot water and a good amount of dish soap. Let the bottles soak 20 to 60 minutes. This is usually better for loosening label adhesive than bleach.</detail>

<step>3. Peel what you can, then remove adhesive.</step>
<detail>If labels do not come off cleanly, use rubbing alcohol, hand sanitizer, cooking oil, or an adhesive remover on the remaining glue. Let it sit briefly, then scrub with a rag or non-scratch scrubber.</detail>

<step>4. For labels that are fused on, destroy the information instead of chasing a perfect peel.</step>
<detail>If a label will not come off, cut that section out with scissors, or shred the labeled part if the plastic is thin enough. Another option is to crush the bottle and cut through the label text so the information is no longer readable.</detail>

<step>5. Separate bottle and cap if required by local recycling.</step>
<detail>Some programs accept prescription bottles, some do not. Check your local recycling rules. If they are not accepted, you can still discard them once the identifying information is removed or destroyed.</detail>

If you have many bottles, the fastest privacy-first option is often:
<detail>soak in hot soapy water → peel what comes off → cut out or destroy any stubborn labeled areas → recycle or trash according to local rules.</detail>

If your pharmacy participates in bottle reuse or take-back for empties, ask them first. Some pharmacies or charities accept clean bottles, but only if labels are fully removed and local rules allow it.

response:
Stop contacting him for now.

The key issue is no longer whether he had a good excuse on a given day. The key issue is that, by your own description, this is part of a pattern: unresolved conflict, missed call, silence, and no response even after you disclosed a major family emergency. Whether that silence comes from illness, avoidance, overwhelm, or indifference, the practical result is the same: he is not functioning like a reliable partner when it matters.

Do not send another explanatory text, do not argue your case, and do not try to force closure in real time. If he reaches out later, do not jump straight into comforting him or resuming normal conversation. Address the behavior directly. Keep it simple: he disappeared during an unresolved conflict and remained unavailable when you told him about a serious family crisis. Ask whether he intends to continue this relationship and whether he is willing to communicate in a basic, respectful way going forward.

If he ghosts you entirely, treat that as your answer. You do not need his formal statement to recognize that a relationship is effectively over when one person repeatedly withdraws instead of communicating.

Also, be careful with your own certainty about what he saw or why he did what he did. You do not actually know whether he read, processed, or was capable of replying in that moment. What you do know is enough: he did not respond. That is the fact to base decisions on. You do not need to prove malicious intent to decide his behavior is unacceptable to you.

Right now, redirect your energy toward your family, especially your mother, and toward people who are actually available to support you. If friends or relatives are responsive, lean on them instead of waiting by your phone for him.

If he does come back, judge him by accountability, not by excuses. A worthwhile response would include a clear acknowledgment of his absence, a real explanation, and changed behavior. Anything less is likely a continuation of the same pattern.

<response>
Stop contacting him for now.

The key issue is no longer whether he had a good excuse on a given day. The key issue is that, by your own description, this is part of a pattern: unresolved conflict, missed call, silence, and no response even after you disclosed a major family emergency. Whether that silence comes from illness, avoidance, overwhelm, or indifference, the practical result is the same: he is not functioning like a reliable partner when it matters.

Do not send another explanatory text, do not argue your case, and do not try to force closure in real time. If he reaches out later, do not jump straight into comforting him or resuming normal conversation. Address the behavior directly. Keep it simple: he disappeared during an unresolved conflict and remained unavailable when you told him about a serious family crisis. Ask whether he intends to continue this relationship and whether he is willing to communicate in a basic, respectful way going forward.

If he ghosts you entirely, treat that as your answer. You do not need his formal statement to recognize that a relationship is effectively over when one person repeatedly withdraws instead of communicating.

Also, be careful with your own certainty about what he saw or why he did what he did. You do not actually know whether he read, processed, or was capable of replying in that moment. What you do know is enough: he did not respond. That is the fact to base decisions on. You do not need to prove malicious intent to decide his behavior is unacceptable to you.

Right now, redirect your energy toward your family, especially your mother, and toward people who are actually available to support you. If friends or relatives are responsive, lean on them instead of waiting by your phone for him.

If he does come back, judge him by accountability, not by excuses. A worthwhile response would include a clear acknowledgment of his absence, a real explanation, and changed behavior. Anything less is likely a continuation of the same pattern.
</response>

response:
<advice>You should treat this as over and stop pursuing any further contact, including through friends. His behavior already answered the question: he avoided you, would not speak plainly, and then blocked you. Whether he was cowardly, confused, or careless does not change the practical reality.</advice>
  <advice>The part you should change going forward is involving other people. Asking his friend put someone else in the middle and usually makes breakups messier, not clearer. If someone will not respond directly, the better move is one final message and then no more contact.</advice>
  <advice>A cleaner approach would have been: “Your silence and blocking tell me this relationship is over. I’m not contacting you again. Goodbye.” Since you already sent a goodbye, stick to it now.</advice>
  <advice>For sleep and the immediate physical crash you describe, focus on reducing activation rather than solving the relationship in your head. Do these tonight: put your phone out of reach, mute or block his accounts so you stop checking, do not look at his Instagram, eat something simple, drink water, shower, and lie down with a podcast or boring audio instead of scrolling. If your thoughts start looping, write one sentence on paper: “It is over, and I do not need more proof tonight.” Repeat that instead of reopening the story.</advice>
  <advice>Over the next few days, ask one trusted friend or family member to stay in close contact with you, not to investigate him, but to help you eat, sleep, and keep your routine. If you feel so weak that you cannot sleep at all, cannot eat, or feel panicky nonstop, reach out to a doctor or mental health professional promptly.</advice>
  <advice>For future relationships, set a clear standard early: if someone will be offline for work, you need agreed expectations for communication. If they can post publicly but not answer you for nearly two weeks, that is not ignorance about texting norms; it is avoidance.</advice>

<advice>
    <point>You need to stop treating this as a question of whether you are being nice enough. The current arrangement is not acceptable. A guest has turned into an unpaid roommate, and you have been displaced from your own bedroom.</point>
    <point>Your immediate task is to be clear, not subtle. Tell your boyfriend plainly: “I am no longer willing to host him. He needs to leave by a specific date.” Do not frame this as a complaint about curtains or burping. The real issue is that the stay is over, your consent is withdrawn, and your home is no longer functioning as your home.</point>
    <point>Set a firm deadline, not an open-ended discussion. For example: “He was invited for 1–2 weeks. It has been over a month. He needs to be out within 3 days” or whatever short deadline is realistic in your area. If your boyfriend says he “can’t” kick him out, respond to that directly: “Then I will tell him myself, because I am not agreeing to continue this.”</point>
    <point>Speak to the friend directly if your boyfriend will not. Keep it brief and factual: “When we agreed to host you, it was for 1–2 weeks. It has now been over a month, and this is no longer working for me. You need to make other arrangements and move out by [date].” You do not need to litigate every annoyance unless he argues. If he does, repeat the deadline.</point>
    <point>Also set immediate house boundaries for the remaining days: “Do not come into my study while I’m working unless invited. Do not use my slippers. Keep the curtains open. We will eat on our own schedule.” These are simple, concrete rules.</point>
    <point>The bedroom issue needs correction tonight. Sleep in your own bed. If your boyfriend wants his friend to stay a few more days, then they can sort out where the friend sleeps without removing you from your bedroom. You walking on eggshells in your own home at 6 AM is not a reason for you to lose your bed.</point>
    <point>More broadly, your boyfriend is the bigger problem now. Not because he invited a friend once, but because after seeing your distress, he chose avoidance over protecting your shared home and your place in it. Pay attention to that. A partner should not leave you crying in the study while he sleeps with his guest in your bedroom and laughs off your concerns.</point>
    <point>If you feel unsafe or think either man will ignore you, involve practical support: a landlord if lease rules prohibit extended guests, a trusted friend or family member, or make arrangements to stay elsewhere temporarily while you decide your next step. But if safety is not the issue, direct communication and a hard deadline are overdue.</point>
  </advice>

response:
You need to treat this as both a safety problem and a treatment-structure problem, not a willpower problem.

First: because you’re having suicidal thoughts and you’re sometimes not eating or drinking, get immediate human support today, especially if you might act on the thoughts, can’t keep yourself safe, or are going long periods without food or fluids. Contact your local crisis line or emergency services now, or go to the nearest ER/urgent psychiatric service. If you’re in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988. If elsewhere, contact your country’s crisis service now. If possible, tell one real person directly: “I’m having suicidal thoughts and I don’t feel safe being alone.”

Until you have support in place, do the following as concretely as possible:
- Do not stay completely alone with this.
- Move anything you could use to hurt yourself farther away or give it to someone else to hold.
- Drink some water or electrolyte drink now, even a few sips.
- Eat the easiest thing available, even if it’s small.
- Sit near another person, or stay on a call/text with someone, or go to a staffed public place if that is safer than being alone at home.

Second: given how severe and long-lasting this has been, outpatient weekly therapy by itself may not be enough. Ask specifically for a higher level of care or a more targeted evaluation:
- a psychiatric review of your diagnoses and medications
- an intensive outpatient program (IOP), partial hospitalization program (PHP), or community mental health team
- treatment specifically for panic/agoraphobia/social anxiety and OCD, such as CBT with exposure and response prevention
- assessment for whether depression, trauma, autism, or another condition is also contributing, if that has not been carefully evaluated

When you contact a provider, be very direct:
“I’m mostly housebound, I have panic attacks when I go out, I’ve had suicidal thoughts for years, and I sometimes don’t eat or drink. Weekly therapy hasn’t been enough. I need a higher level of care or urgent psychiatric evaluation.”

Third: to break the routine, stop aiming for “go out and function normally.” Your current cycle is:
stay in → feel worse/suicidal
go out too hard → panic/crash
crash → avoid more

So the target is not bravery; it is tiny, repeatable, non-catastrophic steps. Examples:
- Stand at the front door for 30 seconds.
- Open the door and breathe for 1 minute.
- Step outside for 1 minute, then back in.
- Walk to the end of the path/street and return.
- Repeat the same step daily until it is boring, not until it feels perfect.

Important: don’t judge success by how calm you feel. Judge it by whether you completed the step and stayed with the anxiety long enough for your brain to learn “I can survive this.”

Fourth: reduce the immediate pressure when outside.
- Wear simple clothes you don’t have to think about.
- Use one sentence scripts: “Hi, I’m a bit anxious today.” “Can you repeat that?” “I need a minute.”
- Keep outings extremely short at first.
- Plan a recovery period after going out, but not a full-day collapse if possible.

Fifth: rebuild the basics before expecting productivity.
For the next few days, your job is only:
- drink something 3 times a day
- eat something 3 times a day, even if tiny
- wash or change clothes once
- do one tiny outside step
- contact one support person or service

If reconnecting with a friend feels possible, send a low-pressure message:
“I’ve been struggling badly with anxiety and isolation. I’m trying to reconnect and may be slow to reply, but I wanted to reach out.”

The main point: this is severe enough that you should not try to solve it alone, and “try harder” is the wrong strategy. Get crisis support now if you may be unsafe, and pursue a more intensive, specialized treatment setup rather than another vague round of therapy.

<advice>You do not need to cancel the trip, apologize for supporting your in-laws, or accept the claim that taking grieving parents on holiday means you do not care about your family.</advice>
  <advice>You do need to own the part that is actually yours: you handled the communication poorly. Tell your siblings that directly and narrowly. Something like: “I should have told you myself, and earlier. I can see why hearing it last-minute through Mom hurt.” That is enough. Do not apologize for the trip itself if you do not believe it was wrong.</advice>
  <advice>Then set a boundary around the abusive part. For example: “I’m willing to talk about hurt feelings, but I’m not willing to be insulted or accused of not caring about the family. If you want to talk respectfully, I’m open to that after I get back.” This addresses the texts without escalating to your parents.</advice>
  <advice>Do not use your parents as enforcers unless the messages become threatening or severely abusive. Right now, if the issue is angry guilt-tripping, the better move is to respond yourself once, clearly, and stop the back-and-forth.</advice>
  <advice>It would also be wise to send one group message rather than litigating this sibling by sibling. Keep it short: you are taking your in-laws away because of Gabriel’s death, you should have communicated earlier and directly, and you will discuss family feelings after the holiday if they can do so respectfully.</advice>
  <advice>After the trip, decide whether you want a broader conversation about the longstanding distance with your family. Their reaction suggests this is not only about Christmas. If you want that relationship improved, address the bigger pattern later, separately from this immediate conflict. If you do not want deeper involvement, then be honest with yourself and set expectations accordingly instead of drifting into distance and letting each holiday reopen the wound.</advice>
  <advice>For now: go on the trip, mute the chaotic threads, give one calm response, and refuse to defend a compassionate decision beyond acknowledging that your delivery was hurtful.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You do not need to cancel the trip, apologize for supporting your in-laws, or accept the claim that taking grieving parents on holiday means you do not care about your family.</advice>
  <advice>You do need to own the part that is actually yours: you handled the communication poorly. Tell your siblings that directly and narrowly. Something like: “I should have told you myself, and earlier. I can see why hearing it last-minute through Mom hurt.” That is enough. Do not apologize for the trip itself if you do not believe it was wrong.</advice>
  <advice>Then set a boundary around the abusive part. For example: “I’m willing to talk about hurt feelings, but I’m not willing to be insulted or accused of not caring about the family. If you want to talk respectfully, I’m open to that after I get back.” This addresses the texts without escalating to your parents.</advice>
  <advice>Do not use your parents as enforcers unless the messages become threatening or severely abusive. Right now, if the issue is angry guilt-tripping, the better move is to respond yourself once, clearly, and stop the back-and-forth.</advice>
  <advice>It would also be wise to send one group message rather than litigating this sibling by sibling. Keep it short: you are taking your in-laws away because of Gabriel’s death, you should have communicated earlier and directly, and you will discuss family feelings after the holiday if they can do so respectfully.</advice>
  <advice>After the trip, decide whether you want a broader conversation about the longstanding distance with your family. Their reaction suggests this is not only about Christmas. If you want that relationship improved, address the bigger pattern later, separately from this immediate conflict. If you do not want deeper involvement, then be honest with yourself and set expectations accordingly instead of drifting into distance and letting each holiday reopen the wound.</advice>
  <advice>For now: go on the trip, mute the chaotic threads, give one calm response, and refuse to defend a compassionate decision beyond acknowledging that your delivery was hurtful.</advice>
</response>

response:
<advice>You should stop cleaning his house to this extent, stop hinting, and tell him plainly that you will not move in unless the home becomes consistently clean and safe by his own effort, not yours.</advice>
  <advice>This is not “naggy,” “controlling,” or “OCD.” Based on what you described, this is a basic cohabitation standard: clean enough to walk around safely, use the kitchen hygienically, and not clean someone else’s toilet mess every time you visit.</advice>
  <advice>Do not make it a debate about whether his standards are objectively wrong or whether you are too particular. Keep it on compatibility and conditions for moving in. For example: “I need to tell you the real reason I’m hesitating about moving in. I’m not willing to live in the house as it is now. The level of mess and hygiene is too much for me, and I’m already finding myself cleaning a lot when I come over. If we ever live together, I need a consistently clean and safe home, and I need that not to depend on me doing most of the work.”</advice>
  <advice>Be specific about what “clean and safe” means. Do not rely on vague phrases like “tidier” or “better.” Name the concrete issues you already listed: no rubbish, letters, tools, nails, screws, or wire left on floors; kitchen counters and sink cleaned after use; toilets cleaned regularly; dirty dishes not left to rot; floors cleaned often enough that socks do not get filthy; clutter contained rather than spread through every room.</advice>
  <advice>Then set a boundary rather than volunteering more labor. Something like: “I’m not going to keep doing big cleaning resets for you, and I’m not moving in while this is still the pattern.” That gives him a real choice. He can decide that he wants to change, or he can decide he does not care enough to. Either answer is useful information.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let the discussion get derailed into “but I never asked you to clean.” The answer is: “I know you didn’t. I cleaned because I couldn’t comfortably be there otherwise. That’s exactly why I’m raising it now—because I can’t live like that long term.”</advice>
  <advice>Also do not accept the “you’re just OCD” framing. You do not need to prove a diagnosis or defend your personality. The point is simpler: “Regardless of labels, this living situation doesn’t work for me.”</advice>
  <advice>Before any move-in decision, watch for sustained change over time, not a one-week cleanup prompted by the conversation. If he can independently keep the house at a livable standard for a couple of months, that suggests he is capable of sharing a home with you. If he does one dramatic reset and then slides back, that is your answer.</advice>
  <advice>If he genuinely wants to solve it but struggles with the habit, practical options exist: a chore schedule, a rule that tools and work materials get put away immediately, a weekly reset, bins in key places, or even paying for a cleaner if he can afford it. But those only matter if he accepts that there is a problem and takes ownership of fixing it.</advice>
  <advice>Until then, protect your time and energy. Spend less time at his house if being there turns you into unpaid domestic labor. Do not buy more cleaning supplies as hints. Do not sacrifice holidays and study time doing 20-hour cleanups. You are currently acting like a trial live-in partner without the agreement, respect for your standards, or shared effort that would make that workable.</advice>
  <advice>So the immediate next step is one direct conversation, followed by observation. No excuses, no hints, no more compensating. If the house stays the same, do not move in. If that ends the relationship, it will not be because you were controlling; it will be because the two of you were not compatible enough to share a home.</advice>

<response>
  <advice>You should stop cleaning his house to this extent, stop hinting, and tell him plainly that you will not move in unless the home becomes consistently clean and safe by his own effort, not yours.</advice>
  <advice>This is not “naggy,” “controlling,” or “OCD.” Based on what you described, this is a basic cohabitation standard: clean enough to walk around safely, use the kitchen hygienically, and not clean someone else’s toilet mess every time you visit.</advice>
  <advice>Do not make it a debate about whether his standards are objectively wrong or whether you are too particular. Keep it on compatibility and conditions for moving in. For example: “I need to tell you the real reason I’m hesitating about moving in. I’m not willing to live in the house as it is now. The level of mess and hygiene is too much for me, and I’m already finding myself cleaning a lot when I come over. If we ever live together, I need a consistently clean and safe home, and I need that not to depend on me doing most of the work.”</advice>
  <advice>Be specific about what “clean and safe” means. Do not rely on vague phrases like “tidier” or “better.” Name the concrete issues you already listed: no rubbish, letters, tools, nails, screws, or wire left on floors; kitchen counters and sink cleaned after use; toilets cleaned regularly; dirty dishes not left to rot; floors cleaned often enough that socks do not get filthy; clutter contained rather than spread through every room.</advice>
  <advice>Then set a boundary rather than volunteering more labor. Something like: “I’m not going to keep doing big cleaning resets for you, and I’m not moving in while this is still the pattern.” That gives him a real choice. He can decide that he wants to change, or he can decide he does not care enough to. Either answer is useful information.</advice>
  <advice>Do not let the discussion get derailed into “but I never asked you to clean.” The answer is: “I know you didn’t. I cleaned because I couldn’t comfortably be there otherwise. That’s exactly why I’m raising it now—because I can’t live like that long term.”</advice>
  <advice>Also do not accept the “you’re just OCD” framing. You do not need to prove a diagnosis or defend your personality. The point is simpler: “Regardless of labels, this living situation doesn’t work for me.”</advice>
  <advice>Before any move-in decision, watch for sustained change over time, not a one-week cleanup prompted by the conversation. If he can independently keep the house at a livable standard for a couple of months, that suggests he is capable of sharing a home with you. If he does one dramatic reset and then slides back, that is your answer.</advice>
  <advice>If he genuinely wants to solve it but struggles with the habit, practical options exist: a chore schedule, a rule that tools and work materials get put away immediately, a weekly reset, bins in key places, or even paying for a cleaner if he can afford it. But those only matter if he accepts that there is a problem and takes ownership of fixing it.</advice>
  <advice>Until then, protect your time and energy. Spend less time at his house if being there turns you into unpaid domestic labor. Do not buy more cleaning supplies as hints. Do not sacrifice holidays and study time doing 20-hour cleanups. You are currently acting like a trial live-in partner without the agreement, respect for your standards, or shared effort that would make that workable.</advice>
  <advice>So the immediate next step is one direct conversation, followed by observation. No excuses, no hints, no more compensating. If the house stays the same, do not move in. If that ends the relationship, it will not be because you were controlling; it will be because the two of you were not compatible enough to share a home.</advice>
</response>

<advice>
    <point>Your first move is to find out the exact academic options before the deadline passes. Today, check the syllabus and your college calendar for the withdrawal deadline, pass/fail rules if any, and how a failed or withdrawn class affects GPA, aid, and prerequisites.</point>
    <point>Email your professor now and ask one direct question: given your current grades, is there any realistic path to passing, or should you withdraw? Do not ask for pity; ask for an honest assessment based on the grading scheme.</point>
    <point>Also contact your academic advisor as soon as possible. You need to know whether withdrawing is smarter than taking the F, whether this class is required for your major, and when you can retake it.</point>
    <point>If the professor and advisor indicate passing is realistically out of reach, withdrawing is often better than staying in and collecting an F, assuming it is still allowed and does not create a separate problem for financial aid or full-time status. Verify those details before acting.</point>
    <point>If withdrawal is no longer possible, stop treating this as only a math problem. It is now a course-management problem. You should still meet the professor, learn what topics you are missing, and use the rest of the term to rebuild enough foundation so that retaking the course is easier.</point>
    <point>You also need to tell your family. Keep it simple and factual: you are likely failing math, here is why, here is what you are doing this week to address it, and here is what support you may need. Hiding it further only makes the situation harder.</point>
    <point>For the future, do not repeat the setup that led here. Do not take a 7AM math class if you already know you cannot focus then. Put difficult quantitative courses at times when you are actually alert.</point>

response:
You need to treat this as a body-image adjustment problem, not as proof that your progress is fake.

Your body changed faster than your self-concept did. That is common. People often assume confidence should automatically appear after weight loss, but the mind can keep running an old script long after circumstances change.

Do a few things deliberately:

<step>Stop using your former body as your identity. "I used to be heavier" is a fact. "I am still that unattractive person" is a conclusion, not a fact.</step>

<step>Use objective markers, not mood, to judge reality. Track things like energy, strength, labs, sleep, how clothes fit, photos over time, and what you can physically do now that you could not do before. Your feelings matter, but they are not the only evidence.</step>

<step>Update your mental image on purpose. Look at recent photos regularly, not compulsively. Compare them with older ones. Let your brain repeatedly see the current version of you. Mirrors can be distorted by emotion; photos and measurements can help ground you.</step>

<step>Watch your self-talk closely. If you catch yourself saying "I’m still that heavy unattractive person," replace it with something accurate: "I’m healthier than before, and my mind hasn’t fully caught up yet." The goal is not fake positivity; it is accuracy.</step>

<step>Do not make confidence depend entirely on appearance. Build it from actions: keeping promises to yourself, staying consistent, getting stronger, being socially present, dressing well, sleeping enough, and taking care of your health. Appearance-based confidence is fragile by itself.</step>

<step>If relationships were affected by your old self-image, work on the relational side too. Practice accepting compliments without arguing. Practice saying what you feel directly instead of asking other people to constantly disprove your insecurity.</step>

<step>Set a line where "health improvement" ends and "chasing worth" begins. If you find yourself thinking that just a little more weight loss will finally make you acceptable, that is a warning sign. The problem may no longer be your body; it may be how you evaluate yourself.</step>

If this feeling is persistent, strong, or starts affecting eating, exercise, dating, or daily functioning, talk to a therapist—especially one familiar with body image or self-esteem issues. Losing weight fixes some problems, but it does not automatically heal the beliefs you built while living in the old body.

Your task now is not to become a different person. It is to let your mind catch up to what you have already done.

<step>Update your mental image on purpose. Look at recent photos regularly, not compulsively. Compare them with older ones. Let your brain repeatedly see the current version of you. Mirrors can be distorted by emotion; photos and measurements can help ground you.</step>

<step>Watch your self-talk closely. If you catch yourself saying "I’m still that heavy unattractive person," replace it with something accurate: "I’m healthier than before, and my mind hasn’t fully caught up yet." The goal is not fake positivity; it is accuracy.</step>

<step>Do not make confidence depend entirely on appearance. Build it from actions: keeping promises to yourself, staying consistent, getting stronger, being socially present, dressing well, sleeping enough, and taking care of your health. Appearance-based confidence is fragile by itself.</step>

<step>If relationships were affected by your old self-image, work on the relational side too. Practice accepting compliments without arguing. Practice saying what you feel directly instead of asking other people to constantly disprove your insecurity.</step>

<step>Set a line where "health improvement" ends and "chasing worth" begins. If you find yourself thinking that just a little more weight loss will finally make you acceptable, that is a warning sign. The problem may no longer be your body; it may be how you evaluate yourself.</step>

If this feeling is persistent, strong, or starts affecting eating, exercise, dating, or daily functioning, talk to a therapist—especially one familiar with body image or self-esteem issues. Losing weight fixes some problems, but it does not automatically heal the beliefs you built while living in the old body.

Your task now is not to become a different person. It is to let your mind catch up to what you have already done.

<advice>
    Do not break up right before you leave just because the timing is convenient. If you are going to end the relationship, it should be because you have concluded the relationship is not workable, not because a month-long absence creates an easy window.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    Since you have already agreed to therapy, the better course is: do not make a breakup decision before the trip unless there is abuse, threats, or an immediate safety issue. Instead, use the period before and during the trip to set up couples therapy and to make a serious individual plan for your forgetfulness.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    But you need to stop treating this as mainly a problem with her anger. Her anger may be excessive, dysregulated, or corrosive over time, but the relationship problem begins with repeated breaches of reliability and safety that you already expect to continue. If you keep saying, in effect, “I make mistakes, she just reacts badly,” therapy will go nowhere.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    You should tell her something closer to this: “You are right that these lapses affect your sense of safety and trust. I have been focusing too much on your reactions and not enough on the impact of my actions. I need us to work on both: my reliability and how we handle conflict.”
  </advice>
  <advice>
    Then make your effort more concrete. Do not promise to “try harder.” Build systems:
    <item>automatic recurring reminders for bins, doors, and end-of-night checks,</item>
    <item>a written closing checklist for the office and house,</item>
    <item>physical cues at exits,</item>
    <item>division of responsibilities based on what you can actually perform consistently,</item>
    <item>evaluation for ADHD or similar issues, even if you do not want medication.</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>
    On that last point: you do not have to take medication, but you should stop using “I probably have ADHD” as an explanation without fully pursuing assessment and treatment options. Assessment, coaching, therapy, habit design, and if appropriate medication are all on the table. Refusing one option is your choice; refusing to seriously address the condition is not fair to a partner affected by it.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    You also need a different fight strategy. In heated moments, stop saying she hates you, stop asking why she stays, and stop making the conflict about the entire relationship. First acknowledge the concrete issue, then the impact, then the fix. For example: “I left the office unsecured. I understand why that felt unsafe and infuriating. I’m going to put a lock-check routine in place.” That will land much better than apologies mixed with self-defense.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    At the same time, therapy should test a second question plainly: even if you improve, is she willing and able to stop stockpiling resentment and attacking you with the whole history every time you slip? Because if her pattern is chronic contempt, no amount of checklists will save the relationship. Your mistakes are real; perpetual unforgiveness and explosive conflict are also real problems.
  </advice>
  <advice>
    So the practical recommendation is:
    <item>Do not end it before the trip unless there is immediate danger.</item>
    <item>Set up couples therapy now.</item>
    <item>Get professionally assessed for ADHD or whatever is driving the forgetfulness.</item>
    <item>Implement specific reliability systems before you leave.</item>
    <item>When you return, evaluate based on evidence: are your lapses decreasing, and is her way of handling them becoming less hostile?</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>
    If after a real attempt the pattern remains “you keep creating safety/reliability problems” plus “she keeps responding with escalating resentment and contempt,” then the relationship may simply be unworkable, even if you love each other.
  </advice>

response:
Don’t tell them they’re being scammed, and don’t tell them they’re wasting their time. If you do, they’ll hear “you’re stupid,” not “I’m worried about you.”

Instead, do three things:

<point>1. Drop the contempt.</point>
Do not mention that the name is awful, the products look cheap, or that you expected them to have “more sense.” Those thoughts may be real, but saying them serves no useful purpose.

<point>2. Ask questions instead of delivering a verdict.</point>
A better approach is:
<example>“How does the pay structure actually work?”</example>
<example>“Do you have to buy inventory or pay ongoing fees?”</example>
<example>“How much do people typically make after expenses?”</example>
<example>“What happens if you don’t recruit anyone?”</example>

That keeps the conversation on facts. If they haven’t looked closely, the questions may do more than an argument would.

<point>3. Focus on specific risks, not labels.</point>
You can say something like:
<example>“I’m a little wary of businesses where the money depends heavily on recruiting or pushing friends to host sales events. I’d just hate to see you spend money or strain friendships if the returns aren’t there.”</example>

That is much better than:
<example>“This is a scam.”</example>

If they ask what worries you, then be concrete:
<example>“I’ve heard that with businesses like this, a lot of people end up buying starter kits, posting constantly, leaning on friends and family, and making very little after costs. Have you seen the income disclosure or worked out your likely profit?”</example>

<point>4. Respect that they may not be ready to hear it.</point>
People who just joined something like this often need time before they can question it. If they push back, stop. You do not need to win the argument.

<point>5. Set boundaries if they start selling to you.</point>
If your real immediate problem is that they’re trying to recruit or sell through you, say so plainly:
<example>“I want to support you as a friend, but I’m not interested in buying, hosting, or joining.”</example>

That protects you without attacking them.

If you want one short version to use, use this:
<example>“I’m not interested in joining or buying, but I do want to say I’d be careful with any business that relies a lot on recruiting and selling to friends. I’d just want you to look closely at the numbers before investing too much time or money.”</example>

That communicates concern without insulting them.

    <concern>You are approaching this with contempt for the product and brand ("the name is awful, the products look cheap, it's expensive").     <concern>Calling it a "scam" or telling them they are "being scammed" would dismiss their decision outright. Given your stated intent to tell them they are "wasting their time," a blunt accusation is likely to hurt the friendship and reduce the chance they will listen.</concern>

<response>
Don’t tell them they’re being scammed, and don’t tell them they’re wasting their time. If you do, they’ll hear “you’re stupid,” not “I’m worried about you.”

Instead, do three things:

<point>1. Drop the contempt.</point>
Do not mention that the name is awful, the products look cheap, or that you expected them to have “more sense.” Those thoughts may be real, but saying them serves no useful purpose.

<point>2. Ask questions instead of delivering a verdict.</point>
A better approach is:
<example>“How does the pay structure actually work?”</example>
<example>“Do you have to buy inventory or pay ongoing fees?”</example>
<example>“How much do people typically make after expenses?”</example>
<example>“What happens if you don’t recruit anyone?”</example>

That keeps the conversation on facts. If they haven’t looked closely, the questions may do more than an argument would.

<point>3. Focus on specific risks, not labels.</point>
You can say something like:
<example>“I’m a little wary of businesses where the money depends heavily on recruiting or pushing friends to host sales events. I’d just hate to see you spend money or strain friendships if the returns aren’t there.”</example>

That is much better than:
<example>“This is a scam.”</example>

If they ask what worries you, then be concrete:
<example>“I’ve heard that with businesses like this, a lot of people end up buying starter kits, posting constantly, leaning on friends and family, and making very little after costs. Have you seen the income disclosure or worked out your likely profit?”</example>

<point>4. Respect that they may not be ready to hear it.</point>
People who just joined something like this often need time before they can question it. If they push back, stop. You do not need to win the argument.

<point>5. Set boundaries if they start selling to you.</point>
If your real immediate problem is that they’re trying to recruit or sell through you, say so plainly:
<example>“I want to support you as a friend, but I’m not interested in buying, hosting, or joining.”</example>

That protects you without attacking them.

If you want one short version to use, use this:
<example>“I’m not interested in joining or buying, but I do want to say I’d be careful with any business that relies a lot on recruiting and selling to friends. I’d just want you to look closely at the numbers before investing too much time or money.”</example>

That communicates concern without insulting them.
</response>

response:
<advice>
    <point>This needs urgent in-person help. Do not treat this as just needing better habits or motivation. The combination of suicidal fear, not eating or drinking, eating spoiled food, and losing days at a time means you should seek emergency or same-day assessment.</point>

    <point>If you might harm yourself, feel unable to stay safe, or are slipping into another period where you stop eating/drinking or lose touch with reality, call emergency services now or go to the nearest emergency department immediately. If a suicide crisis line is available where you live, call or text it now. If you are in the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988.</point>

    <point>Tell one real person today, in direct language. Do not soften it. Send something like: “I am not safe being alone right now. I have been losing time, not eating or drinking, and I’m scared I may become suicidal. I need you to help me get urgent care today.” Send that to a parent, your girlfriend, a trusted friend, or another family member.</point>

    <point>Do not stay alone with this if you can avoid it. Go stay with family or ask someone to come be with you, especially if you are having another “absent” period. Being around another person may reduce the risk of not eating, not drinking, or disappearing for days.</point>

    <point>Contact your college again, but escalate beyond routine booking. Email and call the counseling center, student affairs/dean of students, campus health clinic, disability office, and any emergency after-hours line. Say clearly that you are having suicidal thoughts/fears, severe self-neglect, and episodes of lost time. Those details matter because they may move you out of the normal queue.</point>

    <point>You also need a medical and psychiatric evaluation. Depression is possible, but “lost time,” feeling unreal, and going days without awareness can also happen with dissociation, trauma-related conditions, severe depression, substance effects, sleep problems, neurological issues, or other medical causes. A proper assessment matters here.</point>

    <point>Until you are seen, reduce immediate physical risk:
      <subpoint>Drink water now. Even small amounts regularly are better than waiting.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do not eat food that has spoiled or smells bad.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Use very simple food: bread, yogurt, fruit, instant oats, peanut butter, soup, meal replacement drinks—things that are easy and safer than storing cooked food for too long.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>If cooking leads to rotten food during bad periods, buy small portions and ready-to-eat items for now.</subpoint>
    </point>

    <point>Make your environment harder to “disappear” inside:
      <subpoint>Set repeating alarms labeled: water, eat, shower, text someone, sleep.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Ask one person to check on you at fixed times every day.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Keep a visible daily checklist with only 3 essentials: drink water, eat once, contact one person.</subpoint>
      <subpoint>If you miss check-ins, that person should call you and, if needed, physically come or alert family.</subpoint>
    </point>

    <point>Because you are missing commitments and going silent for days, send a short message to the people affected: “I’m sorry I disappeared. I’m dealing with a serious mental health problem and periods where I lose track of time. I’m seeking urgent help.” You do not need to explain everything, but you should let them know this is serious.</point>

    <point>Do not conclude from your grandfather or sister that this is simply your inherited fate. Family patterns may increase risk, but what you described is treatable and should be evaluated on its own. The immediate issue is safety and assessment, not proving the root cause first.</point>

    <point>If you want, use this exact script when you contact services: “I am a college student. I have had periods of days where I don’t know what happened, I don’t eat or drink, I neglect hygiene, I have eaten rotten food, and I’m scared I may become suicidal. I need an urgent mental health assessment today.”</point>
  </advice>

response:
You are not wrong for thinking this is bigger than a few Instagram follows. The real question is whether this is a one-off reassurance need, or whether you are being pushed into a pattern where her anxiety becomes your job to manage through increasing concessions.

Do not reduce this to "Should I unfollow or not?" Talk about the principle directly:
1. tell her you understand this genuinely upsets her,
2. tell her you are willing to talk about what specifically makes her feel unsafe,
3. tell her that you do not want a relationship where innocence has to be constantly proven through compliance.

A better version of your position would be:
"I get that this brings up anxiety for you, and I'm not mocking that. But I am not flirting, hiding anything, or pursuing these people. I need us to build trust in a way that doesn't turn into controlling each other's harmless social media connections."

That is different from saying "there's nothing to worry about" or "you're being controlling." Those phrases may be understandable, but they usually make the other person feel dismissed or attacked.

You should also ask a clarifying question: what exactly would unfollowing these women solve for her? If the answer is basically "it would temporarily calm me down," that matters. Temporary relief is not the same as addressing the real issue. If you unfollow these people, the anxiety may just move to the next thing: likes, stories, coworkers, friends, who you meet in person, and so on.

So your options are:

- If this is a limited, discussable boundary and she can talk about it without ultimatums, you can work on a compromise.
- If she insists that your reluctance proves you care more about random women than about her, that is manipulative reasoning and a bad standard.
- If this becomes a repeated demand that you narrow your world to manage her insecurity, then yes, that is a serious red flag about compatibility and control.

Do not leave immediately just because this conflict happened. But do treat it as a meaningful test:
- Can she tolerate a boundary without turning it into "you don't love me enough"?
- Can you discuss her insecurity without contempt or labeling?
- Can both of you distinguish reassurance from surveillance and obedience?

If the answer to those is no, then the issue is not Instagram. The issue is that the relationship may not have enough trust or emotional stability to be healthy.

So: don't cave just to stop the discomfort, and don't jump straight to breakup either. Have one calm, direct conversation about trust, boundaries, and what each of you believes a respectful relationship requires. If she cannot accept a reasonable boundary around harmless follows, then leaving becomes much more justified—not because of Instagram itself, but because of the pattern behind it.

"I get that this brings up anxiety for you, and I'm not mocking that. But I am not flirting, hiding anything, or pursuing these people. I need us to build trust in a way that doesn't turn into controlling each other's harmless social media connections."

That is different from saying "there's nothing to worry about" or "you're being controlling." Those phrases may be understandable, but they usually make the other person feel dismissed or attacked.

You should also ask a clarifying question: what exactly would unfollowing these women solve for her? If the answer is basically "it would temporarily calm me down," that matters. Temporary relief is not the same as addressing the real issue. If you unfollow these people, the anxiety may just move to the next thing: likes, stories, coworkers, friends, who you meet in person, and so on.

So your options are:

- If this is a limited, discussable boundary and she can talk about it without ultimatums, you can work on a compromise.
- If she insists that your reluctance proves you care more about random women than about her, that is manipulative reasoning and a bad standard.
- If this becomes a repeated demand that you narrow your world to manage her insecurity, then yes, that is a serious red flag about compatibility and control.

Do not leave immediately just because this conflict happened. But do treat it as a meaningful test:
- Can she tolerate a boundary without turning it into "you don't love me enough"?
- Can you discuss her insecurity without contempt or labeling?
- Can both of you distinguish reassurance from surveillance and obedience?

If the answer to those is no, then the issue is not Instagram. The issue is that the relationship may not have enough trust or emotional stability to be healthy.

So: don't cave just to stop the discomfort, and don't jump straight to breakup either. Have one calm, direct conversation about trust, boundaries, and what each of you believes a respectful relationship requires. If she cannot accept a reasonable boundary around harmless follows, then leaving becomes much more justified—not because of Instagram itself, but because of the pattern behind it.

<advice>You do not need a constant supply of new stories. Most everyday conversation is not built on big updates. It is built on small observations, follow-ups, shared context, and letting topics branch.</advice>
  <advice>Stop thinking of conversation as “I need a fresh topic.” Think of it as one of these:
    <item>comment on something you both just experienced</item>
    <item>follow up on something they mentioned before</item>
    <item>ask for an opinion, not just a fact</item>
    <item>share a small reaction and let them react back</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Use the environment. In school, you automatically have recurring material:
    <item>classes: assignments, teachers, tests, confusing parts, favorite parts</item>
    <item>people: group projects, clubs, school events, campus news</item>
    <item>routine: commute, lunch, weather, weekend plans, tiredness, schedule changes</item>
    <item>culture: music, games, shows, memes, apps, sports, local stuff</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>What keeps conversation going is usually follow-up. If someone says, “I was up late finishing homework,” do not move on immediately. You can ask:
    <item>“Which class?”</item>
    <item>“Was it hard or did you just procrastinate?”</item>
    <item>“Did you finish?”</item>
    <item>“Is that teacher always like that?”</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Those are not deep questions, but they create momentum. Then the topic naturally widens.</advice>
  <advice>Ask questions that invite preference, judgment, or story:
    <item>“How are you liking that class so far?”</item>
    <item>“What’s been the most annoying part of this week?”</item>
    <item>“Do you actually study well at home, or do you get distracted?”</item>
    <item>“What do you usually do after school?”</item>
    <item>“Have you found any decent lunch here yet?”</item>
    <item>“Are you the type to do work early or last minute?”</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>Also, bring back old threads. If someone mentioned a sibling, a test, a sport, a job, a show, a trip, a pet, or an application, ask about it later. People usually like being remembered, and follow-up makes conversation feel natural instead of random.</advice>
  <advice>Do not underestimate low-stakes chat. Talking about sleep, food, or mornings is fine if you turn it into something slightly more specific:
    <item>not just “What did you eat?” but “What’s your go-to breakfast when you’re late?”</item>
    <item>not just “How did you sleep?” but “Are you someone who can function on five hours or not at all?”</item>
    <item>not just “How’s your morning?” but “Did anything annoying already happen today?”</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>You also do not have to fill every silence. Seeing the same people every day means some interactions will be brief. Familiarity often comes from repeated small exchanges, not nonstop interesting dialogue.</advice>
  <advice>A simple pattern to use:
    <item>Notice: “That class felt longer than usual.”</item>
    <item>Ask: “Did you understand that last part?”</item>
    <item>Relate: “I completely lost track when they switched topics.”</item>
    <item>Follow up: “Are you going to start the assignment tonight or pretend it doesn’t exist?”</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you want, I can also give you a list of 50 school-friendly conversation starters that do not sound forced.</advice>

response:
<advice>You should treat this as a real incompatibility, not a problem to solve by waiting longer.</advice>
  <advice>If he wants children in the near future and you do not want them now and may never want them, neither of you is wrong, but you are not aligned on one of the biggest decisions in a long-term relationship.</advice>
  <advice>Do not agree to have a child to “get it over with.” That is a deeply unhealthy way to approach parenthood and would likely harm you, him, and any child involved.</advice>
  <advice>Do not stay in a romantic or intimate situationship while hoping one of you changes. You already have the key information. Staying attached without resolution will only increase pain and pressure.</advice>
  <advice>His suggestion that he have a child with someone else and then be with you is not a workable compromise for most people, and you were right to reject it. If you do not want to date someone with a child, that is your boundary.</advice>
  <advice>On the other hand, he is also allowed to refuse to commit unless he is with someone who actively wants children. That is not something you should try to argue him out of.</advice>
  <advice>Your practical options are basically these:</advice>
  <advice>1. End the romantic and sexual relationship now, because your long-term goals do not match.</advice>
  <advice>2. If you try friendship, it should only happen after real distance and no intimacy, not as a continuation of the same bond under a different label.</advice>
  <advice>3. Only revisit the idea of dating in the future if your view on children changes on its own, not because you fear losing him.</advice>
  <advice>If you stay, you will likely feel pressured; if he stays, he will likely feel he is wasting time on a goal he cares deeply about. That is why ending it is the cleanest choice.</advice>
  <advice>So the next step is to tell him plainly: you care about him, but you cannot promise children, and because of that, you need to stop the relationship-like dynamic instead of continuing in limbo.</advice>

response:
You need a system that decides for you what matters now, instead of one big list that keeps creating guilt.

<steps>
  <step>Split your list into only 3 categories:
    <item>Safety: smoke detector batteries, electrical issues, leaks, anything that could cause damage or risk.</item>
    <item>Prevent expensive damage: furnace filters, water issues, exterior sealing, HVAC maintenance.</item>
    <item>Convenience/cosmetic: annoying but not urgent items.</item>
  </step>
  <step>Always do Safety first, then Prevent expensive damage, then Convenience. If you do nothing else, this solves the “what do I do first?” problem.</step>
  <step>Rewrite each task as the smallest visible next action. Not “fix leaky sink,” but:
    <item>look under sink and identify source</item>
    <item>watch 1 repair video for that faucet model</item>
    <item>buy washer or cartridge</item>
    <item>schedule 20 minutes to install</item>
    Big vague tasks get procrastinated; tiny physical actions get done.</step>
  <step>Use the 15-minute maintenance rule. Set a timer once or twice a week and do only one task or one next action until the timer ends. Stop when it ends. The goal is consistency, not finishing everything.</step>
  <step>Limit your active list. Keep a master list if you want, but only choose 3 current tasks:
    <item>1 safety task</item>
    <item>1 prevention task</item>
    <item>1 easy win</item>
    Ignore the rest until one is completed.</step>
  <step>Put recurring maintenance on a calendar, not on a to-do list. Examples:
    <item>smoke detector batteries: every 6–12 months</item>
    <item>furnace filter: every 1–3 months depending on filter/home</item>
    <item>gutters, HVAC check, seasonal checks: recurring reminders</item>
    If it repeats, automate remembering.</step>
  <step>Define a decision rule for hiring out work. For example:
    <item>if I don’t know how to start after 15 minutes, I get a quote</item>
    <item>if it involves plumbing leaks, electrical, roof, or safety risk beyond basic maintenance, I call a pro</item>
    Some procrastination is really avoidance because the task is unclear or intimidating.</step>
  <step>Batch errands and supplies. Keep a basic home-maintenance bin: batteries, furnace filters, light bulbs, plumber’s tape, screwdriver set. A lot of delay comes from missing one needed item.</step>
  <step>Do a monthly reset:
    <item>cross off completed items</item>
    <item>delete things you no longer need to do</item>
    <item>re-rank what remains by safety, cost prevention, convenience</item>
    This keeps the list from feeling infinite.</step>
</steps>

<simple_priority_method>
  <rule>Ask of each item: can this hurt someone, damage the house, or get more expensive if I wait?</rule>
  <rule>If yes, it moves up.</rule>
  <rule>If no, it can wait.</rule>
</simple_priority_method>

<example>
  <item>Change smoke detector batteries — do first.</item>
  <item>Leaky sink — do next, because water damage gets expensive.</item>
  <item>Replace furnace filter — do next if overdue, because it affects system performance and cost.</item>
  <item>Minor cosmetic annoyance — later.</item>
</example>

Start by choosing one task from your current list that takes under 10 minutes and one task that prevents damage. Do those first, then move recurring items onto a calendar so they stop clogging your list.

response:
<advice>
    <point>Your first job does not require you to feel confident before you start. It requires you to learn a repeatable way to act while nervous. The goal is not “stop being anxious.” The goal is “know what to say and do next even when anxious.”</point>

    <point>Start by separating feelings from predictions. “I feel nervous” is true. “I will fail” is a prediction, not a fact. When the spiral starts, use a short correction: “I am new, not incapable. My job is to handle the next step, not prove everything at once.” Repeat that instead of arguing with every anxious thought.</point>

    <point>Build confidence through scripts. Confidence often comes after repetition, not before it. Write out and practice your most common lines until they sound automatic.</point>

    <point>For walk-ins when no consultant is available, use a calm, firm structure:
      <script>“Welcome. Our showroom is appointment-based, and all consultants are with clients right now. I can do one of three things: check the next available opening, help you schedule an appointment, or take your information so someone can follow up.”</script>
      This works because it does three things: explains the situation, sets a boundary, and gives options.</point>

    <point>If someone gets angry, do not try to win them over emotionally. Keep the interaction structured:
      <script>“I understand this is frustrating. At the moment, no consultant is available immediately. What I can do is book the earliest appointment or take your information for follow-up.”</script>
      If they continue:
      <script>“I understand you want immediate help. I’m not able to interrupt current appointments, but I can help with the next available option.”</script>
      You do not need to become aggressive. You need to become clear and consistent.</point>

    <point>Assertiveness is not being tough or confrontational. It is stating reality clearly without overexplaining or apologizing excessively. Avoid stacking nervous phrases like “um,” “I’m sorry,” “I think,” “maybe,” and “I don’t know.” Replace them with:
      <script>“Here’s what I can do.”</script>
      <script>“The next available option is…”</script>
      <script>“Let me check that for you.”</script>
      <script>“At this time, all consultants are occupied.”</script>
    </point>

    <point>For the phone, slow down by about 15%. Most anxious voices sound uncertain because they speed up, go higher in pitch, and trail off. Before answering, do one breath: inhale 4, exhale 6. Then smile slightly and begin with the same opener every time:
      <script>“Thank you for calling [showroom name], this is [name]. How may I help you?”</script>
      A repeated opener creates steadiness.</point>

    <point>Practice out loud, not just in your head. Spend 10 minutes a day rehearsing:
      <item>your phone greeting</item>
      <item>how to explain appointment-based service</item>
      <item>how to respond to impatience</item>
      <item>how to transfer or escalate questions you cannot answer</item>
