<advice>
    <point>
      Stop having the same broad conversation. Have one structured conversation whose purpose is not to express hurt again, but to decide whether this marriage is going to be actively rebuilt. You need specifics.
    </point>
    <point>
      In that conversation, do not argue about whether he is “trying.” Define observable behaviors. For example:
      <items>
        <item>How many evenings per week are protected couple time, with no last-minute cancellations except genuine emergencies?</item>
        <item>What household responsibilities are fully his, start to finish, without you reminding, planning, or checking?</item>
        <item>How will planning be shared: groceries, appointments, bills, social obligations, trips?</item>
        <item>How much time each week goes to hobbies, friends, family, and the marriage?</item>
      </items>
      If it cannot be observed, it is too vague.
    </point>
    <point>
      Tell him plainly that the issue is not “I want you to give up everything you love.” The issue is that you are consistently getting what is left over, and you are unwilling to remain in a marriage where you are the default manager and lowest priority.
    </point>
    <point>
      Own your part too, but without taking the main burden off him. Say that your withdrawal and letting the home slide are signs that you are burned out and resentful, not a workable long-term strategy. You can say: “I do not want to keep responding by shutting down. I am doing that because I feel hopeless, and that also needs to change.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Propose a short, concrete repair period. For example, 6 to 8 weeks. During that period:
      <items>
        <item>You each have clearly assigned responsibilities.</item>
        <item>You have a weekly check-in for 20 to 30 minutes.</item>
        <item>You track whether commitments actually happened, especially canceled plans and household follow-through.</item>
        <item>You both agree that repeated last-minute deprioritizing of the marriage counts as a failure of the plan.</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      Ask directly for couples counseling now, not later. This is exactly the kind of issue counseling is for: repeated unresolved conversations, different perceptions of effort, and an uneven mental load. If he says he is trying, counseling is a concrete place to show that effort.
    </point>
    <point>
      If he resists structure, avoids counseling, or agrees verbally but still does not follow through in observable ways, then stop treating this as a communication problem. At that point it is a willingness problem. You do not need a sixth or seventh emotional discussion to establish that.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also make your boundary explicit. Not a threat, not drama, just clarity. Something like: “I am willing to work on this seriously with you, but I am not willing to stay indefinitely in a marriage where I carry the relationship and household while being repeatedly deprioritized.” A boundary matters because otherwise he can continue treating your pain as something survivable rather than something requiring change.
    </point>
    <point>
      In the meantime, do not resume being the overfunctioning partner just to keep the peace. But also do not keep using total disengagement as your position. Shift to a cleaner middle ground:
      <items>
        <item>Do your own fair share, not his.</item>
        <item>Do not remind him endlessly.</item>
        <item>Do not rescue tasks he said he would own.</item>
        <item>Keep your own routines and self-care.</item>
        <item>Participate in the structured repair effort if he actually participates.</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      The first step is not “convince him harder.” The first step is to move from repeated pain-based conversations to a concrete plan with a timeline, counseling, and clear consequences if nothing materially changes.
    </point>
  </advice>

  <advice>
    <point>
      Stop having the same broad conversation. Have one structured conversation whose purpose is not to express hurt again, but to decide whether this marriage is going to be actively rebuilt. You need specifics.
    </point>
    <point>
      In that conversation, do not argue about whether he is “trying.” Define observable behaviors. For example:
      <items>
        <item>How many evenings per week are protected couple time, with no last-minute cancellations except genuine emergencies?</item>
        <item>What household responsibilities are fully his, start to finish, without you reminding, planning, or checking?</item>
        <item>How will planning be shared: groceries, appointments, bills, social obligations, trips?</item>
        <item>How much time each week goes to hobbies, friends, family, and the marriage?</item>
      </items>
      If it cannot be observed, it is too vague.
    </point>
    <point>
      Tell him plainly that the issue is not “I want you to give up everything you love.” The issue is that you are consistently getting what is left over, and you are unwilling to remain in a marriage where you are the default manager and lowest priority.
    </point>
    <point>
      Own your part too, but without taking the main burden off him. Say that your withdrawal and letting the home slide are signs that you are burned out and resentful, not a workable long-term strategy. You can say: “I do not want to keep responding by shutting down. I am doing that because I feel hopeless, and that also needs to change.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Propose a short, concrete repair period. For example, 6 to 8 weeks. During that period:
      <items>
        <item>You each have clearly assigned responsibilities.</item>
        <item>You have a weekly check-in for 20 to 30 minutes.</item>
        <item>You track whether commitments actually happened, especially canceled plans and household follow-through.</item>
        <item>You both agree that repeated last-minute deprioritizing of the marriage counts as a failure of the plan.</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      Ask directly for couples counseling now, not later. This is exactly the kind of issue counseling is for: repeated unresolved conversations, different perceptions of effort, and an uneven mental load. If he says he is trying, counseling is a concrete place to show that effort.
    </point>
    <point>
      If he resists structure, avoids counseling, or agrees verbally but still does not follow through in observable ways, then stop treating this as a communication problem. At that point it is a willingness problem. You do not need a sixth or seventh emotional discussion to establish that.
    </point>
    <point>
      Also make your boundary explicit. Not a threat, not drama, just clarity. Something like: “I am willing to work on this seriously with you, but I am not willing to stay indefinitely in a marriage where I carry the relationship and household while being repeatedly deprioritized.” A boundary matters because otherwise he can continue treating your pain as something survivable rather than something requiring change.
    </point>
    <point>
      In the meantime, do not resume being the overfunctioning partner just to keep the peace. But also do not keep using total disengagement as your position. Shift to a cleaner middle ground:
      <items>
        <item>Do your own fair share, not his.</item>
        <item>Do not remind him endlessly.</item>
        <item>Do not rescue tasks he said he would own.</item>
        <item>Keep your own routines and self-care.</item>
        <item>Participate in the structured repair effort if he actually participates.</item>
      </items>
    </point>
    <point>
      The first step is not “convince him harder.” The first step is to move from repeated pain-based conversations to a concrete plan with a timeline, counseling, and clear consequences if nothing materially changes.
    </point>
  </advice>
</response>

You should treat this as a coordination and intimacy-style mismatch, not as a referendum on who is right.

Be very explicit with her outside the bedroom: “I like kissing you. I’m not avoiding kissing or closeness. The specific thing that throws me off is active French kissing during penetration, because I lose rhythm and focus. I still want closeness then, just in a different form.”

That framing matters, because what she is likely hearing is “he doesn’t want intimacy at the moment I most want it,” while what you mean is “I do want intimacy, but this exact version breaks my concentration.”

Then negotiate concretely instead of vaguely. For example:
- Kiss deeply before penetration.
- During PIV, use the forms of contact that work for you: lips together without much motion, forehead-to-forehead, face in her neck, kissing her neck, hair, cheek, or pressing your faces together.
- Add brief kissing pauses rather than continuous French kissing while thrusting.
- If a certain position makes kissing easier without disrupting you, use that position for the moments when she wants more mouth-to-mouth contact.

You can even make it a shared pattern:
- start with kissing,
- transition into penetration,
- maintain close face contact in a way that doesn’t derail you,
- pause occasionally for a few stronger kisses,
- then resume.

That gives her the closeness cue she wants without requiring you to multitask in a way that feels awkward.

Also, don’t oversell the “it probably looks ridiculous” part. The important issue is not appearance; it’s that it interferes with your experience. If you frame it as embarrassment, she may hear shame or rejection. If you frame it as “I can’t stay present in my body and rhythm,” that is easier to work with.

Ask her what exactly she is missing when you do not French kiss during PIV. It may be:
- eye contact,
- feeling wanted,
- face closeness,
- romance,
- synchronization,
- reassurance.

If you know the actual need, you can meet that need in another way. For example:
- If she wants closeness, stay face-to-face and hold her.
- If she wants reassurance, tell her what you feel during penetration.
- If she wants intensity, kiss her between thrusting sequences or during slower moments.
- If she wants connection, use eye contact, touch, and words.

The likely compromise is not “one of you gives in,” but “you build a version of during-sex closeness that works for both of you.” Since you already enjoy kissing in general and want to stay close during PIV, this is a fairly workable mismatch.

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Do not look for a crime to commit. I can’t help with getting jailed on purpose or planning around hidden money. Jail is not a safe or reliable way to get medical care, housing stability, or a restart, and it can leave you with criminal consequences that make all of those problems worse.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your situation sounds urgent because it combines pain, loss of income, lack of heat/hot water, and a sense that you have nothing to lose. Treat it like a crisis in basic needs, not a criminal-planning problem.
    </point>
    <point>
      Get immediate help for the housing conditions. If your heat or water is out, report it to your landlord in writing right away and keep copies. If they do not fix it promptly, contact local tenant enforcement, housing code, legal aid, or a tenants’ union in your area. Lack of heat and water may violate habitability rules.
    </point>
    <point>
      For the knee, use urgent lawful care routes instead of waiting passively for a distant PCP appointment. Call community health clinics, federally qualified health centers, urgent care centers, county hospitals, or hospital financial-assistance offices and ask specifically about low-cost evaluation for an ongoing knee injury after loss of employment. Many areas also have nurse advice lines or charity-care screening.
    </point>
    <point>
      Ask the clinic that turned you away whether they can place you on a cancellation list, suggest a direct-access PT option if your state allows it, or route you to a clinician who can issue the referral sooner. Also ask whether your former PCP office can triage the knee pain without a full new-patient wait.
    </point>
    <point>
      For food, warmth, and short-term stability, contact local shelters, warming centers, mutual-aid groups, food pantries, and 2-1-1 if available where you live. Tell them plainly: no heat/hot water, unemployed, alone, worsening knee pain. That combination often qualifies for emergency help faster than people expect.
    </point>
    <point>
      If your thoughts are drifting from “jail would be easier” toward wanting to get caught, wanting to disappear, or feeling like you may do something reckless because you have nothing to lose, contact crisis support now. In the U.S. or Canada, call or text 988. If you are elsewhere, contact local emergency or crisis services. If you might act today, go to the nearest emergency department or call emergency services.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical next step is to make four calls today: your landlord in writing about heat/water, a local clinic or urgent care about the knee, 2-1-1 or equivalent for emergency basic-needs support, and legal aid or tenant support about the apartment conditions. That is far more likely to help than trying to engineer an arrest.
    </point>
  </advice>

response:
Tell them clearly, privately, and with low pressure.

A good way to do it is:
“I’ve started to see you as more than a friend, and I wanted to be honest about that. If you’d ever want to go on a date, I’d like that. If not, I respect that and I don’t want to make things weird.”

That works because it does three things:
- says what you feel
- makes an actual invitation
- gives them room to say no without feeling trapped

A few practical points:
- Do it one-on-one, not over a group hangout.
- Be specific enough that they know you mean a date, not vague flirting.
- Don’t unload a huge long confession. Keep it simple.
- Ask when you can handle either answer calmly.

Possible responses are usually one of these:
- yes, they’ve felt it too
- maybe / they need time
- no, they only want friendship

If they say yes, great—talk openly about whether you want to take it slowly, especially since you’re already good friends.

If they say no, the important part is to accept it cleanly:
- don’t argue
- don’t ask repeatedly
- don’t punish them with distance unless you genuinely need a little time to reset, in which case say that plainly and respectfully

If you’re especially worried about preserving the friendship, you can make that explicit:
“Our friendship matters to me, so if you’re not interested, I’ll respect that.”

In general, the best transition from friendship to dating is not some perfect dramatic moment. It’s honest, calm, direct communication with enough maturity to handle either outcome. If you want, I can also help you draft a version that sounds more casual, more confident, or more text-message friendly.

<advice>
    <point>If you want the feelings to fade, stop feeding them. Crushes usually stay alive through fantasy, hope, and extra attention.</point>
    <point>Do not treat every interaction as emotionally significant. Keep being friendly, but make your behavior a little more ordinary and less keyed-up.</point>
    <point>Create some distance where you can, even if you cannot avoid seeing her. You do not need to stop being friends, but you can reduce one-on-one time, late-night talks, constant texting, or situations that make the bond feel more intimate than you want.</point>
    <point>Cut off the mental habit of imagining a future with her. When you notice yourself replaying conversations or building scenarios, interrupt it and redirect your attention to something concrete.</point>
    <point>Put more energy into other people and other routines. Spend time with different friends, join activities, study elsewhere, and widen your social world so she is not the emotional center of your day.</point>
    <point>If part of the crush is coming from proximity and familiarity, accept that daily exposure will slow the process. That does not mean you are failing; it just means you need consistency.</point>
    <point>Do not confess just to relieve yourself if you already know you do not want a relationship and want to preserve the friendship. That would mainly shift the emotional burden onto her without solving the core issue.</point>
    <point>It may help to get specific with yourself about why you do not want a relationship with her. A crush can feel powerful when it stays vague. Clarity often weakens it.</point>
    <point>If the feelings stay intense, set firmer internal boundaries: no flirting, no fishing for special attention, no prioritizing her over your own stability.</point>
    <point>Your goal is not to force yourself to feel nothing immediately. Your goal is to behave in ways that let the feelings cool down over time.</point>
  </advice>

response:
You are not overreacting. Based on what you described, this was not just a private crush he managed responsibly. It was an actively cultivated intimate connection with someone he was attracted to, combined with concealment. The lie about being at dinner with a friend when he was actually on a date with you is especially important. That moves this out of the territory of "harmless."

A useful distinction is:

<harmless_crush>
  <point>A harmless crush is noticed, contained, and managed.</point>
  <point>The person keeps appropriate boundaries.</point>
  <point>They do not increase contact, seek special alone time, hide interactions, or build emotional dependency.</point>
</harmless_crush>

<emotional_affair>
  <point>An emotional affair usually involves secrecy, specialness, escalating intimacy, and energy that is being diverted from the primary relationship.</point>
  <point>Your examples fit that pattern: constant texting, emotional closeness, "miss you" messages, one-on-one plans, compliments with romantic undertones, and lying by omission or direct misrepresentation.</point>
</emotional_affair>

So the main issue is not that he found another person appealing. The issue is that once he knew there was attraction, he kept feeding it.

What to do next depends on whether you are trying to evaluate reconciliation or decide whether this is a dealbreaker. Before Sunday, get clear on that for yourself. You do not need to promise him anything at that meeting. You only need to decide what information you need.

On Sunday, stay focused on facts and requirements rather than on whether he "really loves you." Love is not the useful question here. The useful questions are whether he understands what he did, whether he is minimizing it, whether he is willing to create real boundaries, and whether you even want to rebuild trust after this.

Ask questions like:

<questions>
  <question>When did this start crossing the line for you, if ever?</question>
  <question>Why did you tell her you were with friend X instead of saying you were with me?</question>
  <question>Did she know you had a crush on her, either explicitly or implicitly?</question>
  <question>What exactly have you told her now?</question>
  <question>What concrete steps are you willing to take at work, given that you still see her every day?</question>
  <question>Do you understand why I see this as emotional cheating?</question>
  <question>Are you telling the full truth now, or am I going to learn more later?</question>
</questions>

If you are open to repair, do not leave it at "figure it out." Set conditions. For example:

<possible_conditions>
  <condition>No contact outside what is strictly necessary for work.</condition>
  <condition>No private texting, deleting, side channels, or hidden communication.</condition>

response:
Stop trying to "convince" them in the abstract. Shift from vague requests to a clear group process.

<steps>
  <step>Call a short meeting and frame the issue around the project, not their character: "We need a clear plan so the work gets done on time. Let's divide responsibilities and set deadlines."</step>
  <step>Make the workload explicit. Break the project into concrete tasks, assign an owner to each task, and agree on deadlines together. Ask, don't dictate: "Which part can you realistically take?" That avoids sounding like you are ordering peers around.</step>
  <step>Test whether their reasons are real constraints or avoidance. If someone pushes back, ask one follow-up question: "What can you commit to by Thursday?" This keeps you from dismissing everything as an excuse while still requiring accountability.</step>
  <step>Document the plan in writing. Send a brief message listing tasks, owners, and due dates. Professionalism often comes from clarity and records, not from sounding nice.</step>
  <step>Use direct follow-up, not repeated pleading. Example: "You said you'd send the draft by today. Is that still happening? If not, when exactly?"</step>
  <step>If someone does not deliver after a clear agreement, adjust based on consequences rather than emotion. Reassign the task if necessary, keep evidence of who did what, and if this is for school or work, involve the instructor/manager early with facts, not accusations.</step>
</steps>

<what_to_avoid>
  <item>Do not keep making broad requests like "please help more."</item>
  <item>Do not label their responses as excuses in the conversation.</item>
  <item>Do not silently absorb the extra work and then resent them later.</item>
  <item>Do not jump straight to confrontation before roles and deadlines are explicit.</item>
</what_to_avoid>

<phrases>
  <phrase>"We need clear ownership for each part. Who is taking what?"</phrase>
  <phrase>"What can you realistically finish by [date]?"</phrase>
  <phrase>"Let's write this down so we're all aligned."</phrase>
  <phrase>"If you can't take that section, say so now and we'll redistribute it."</phrase>
  <phrase>"If this deadline slips, I'll need to flag it so expectations are clear."</phrase>
</phrases>

Being less of a pushover does not mean becoming harsh. It means being specific, asking for commitments, documenting them, and escalating when agreed work is not done.

response:
<advice>
    <point>
      Stop treating friendliness as evidence of a pending friendship. Walking after class, eating once, texting, and attending hangouts are openings, not proof. A friendship is forming only when the other person also initiates, follows up, includes you, and seems to want contact outside the original setting.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use reciprocity as your main rule. Reach out once or twice. If they respond warmly and sometimes initiate back, continue. If they are polite but don’t initiate, don’t chase. If they stop responding, stop. This is the biggest adjustment you need.
    </point>
    <point>
      Drop the idea that showing up a lot should earn closeness. Attendance helps, but it does not create intimacy by itself. Friendship usually grows from repeated small exchanges of interest, vulnerability, and mutual initiative, not from being present at every event.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop using photos and social media as your scoreboard. Group selfies are not a reliable measure of closeness. If you keep watching for visual proof that you “count,” you will become more anxious and more likely to misread everything else.
    </point>
    <point>
      Build friendships by moving from group presence to specific, low-pressure one-on-one plans. After a good conversation, say something simple like: “I’m grabbing coffee before class Thursday if you want to join,” or “Want to study together for an hour this week?” Then watch what happens next. Do they accept? Reschedule if busy? Later invite you to something? That tells you more than vague friendliness does.
    </point>
    <point>
      In groups, focus less on being included by the whole group and more on forming 1–2 individual bonds inside it. Groups often feel closed until you have a couple of direct connections. Talk to one person before or after events, ask about something specific in their life, and follow up on that later.
    </point>
    <point>
      You may also be holding yourself too tightly. Witty one-liners can help, but they do not create closeness on their own. Closeness usually comes from warmth, curiosity, remembering details, asking follow-up questions, sharing a little about yourself, and giving people room instead of pushing for a certain status.
    </point>
    <point>
      With the girl from class: treat that as a finished casual connection unless she starts re-engaging. One follow-up after the quarter is fine. Repeated attempts after silence are not. The lesson is not “I did everything wrong,” but “friendly weekly contact in a class context does not necessarily continue after the context ends.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Watch your internal language. “Orbiter,” “ostracized,” and comparisons with other awkward people will make you approach friendships as a grievance. Replace that with a simpler question: “Is this person reciprocating?” If yes, invest. If no, step back without turning it into a verdict on your worth.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical filter:
      <subpoint>Do they ever initiate contact?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they ask you questions back?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they accept or suggest plans?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they include you outside the original context?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do you feel more relaxed after interacting, rather than confused and scorekeeping?</subpoint>
      If most answers are no, keep it casual and move on.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your goal should not be “convert acquaintances into friends.” Your goal should be “find the people who naturally reciprocate and invest there.” That shift will make you less intense, more accurate, and more likely to actually form the friendships you want.
    </point>
  </advice>

<response>
  <advice>
    <point>
      Stop treating friendliness as evidence of a pending friendship. Walking after class, eating once, texting, and attending hangouts are openings, not proof. A friendship is forming only when the other person also initiates, follows up, includes you, and seems to want contact outside the original setting.
    </point>
    <point>
      Use reciprocity as your main rule. Reach out once or twice. If they respond warmly and sometimes initiate back, continue. If they are polite but don’t initiate, don’t chase. If they stop responding, stop. This is the biggest adjustment you need.
    </point>
    <point>
      Drop the idea that showing up a lot should earn closeness. Attendance helps, but it does not create intimacy by itself. Friendship usually grows from repeated small exchanges of interest, vulnerability, and mutual initiative, not from being present at every event.
    </point>
    <point>
      Stop using photos and social media as your scoreboard. Group selfies are not a reliable measure of closeness. If you keep watching for visual proof that you “count,” you will become more anxious and more likely to misread everything else.
    </point>
    <point>
      Build friendships by moving from group presence to specific, low-pressure one-on-one plans. After a good conversation, say something simple like: “I’m grabbing coffee before class Thursday if you want to join,” or “Want to study together for an hour this week?” Then watch what happens next. Do they accept? Reschedule if busy? Later invite you to something? That tells you more than vague friendliness does.
    </point>
    <point>
      In groups, focus less on being included by the whole group and more on forming 1–2 individual bonds inside it. Groups often feel closed until you have a couple of direct connections. Talk to one person before or after events, ask about something specific in their life, and follow up on that later.
    </point>
    <point>
      You may also be holding yourself too tightly. Witty one-liners can help, but they do not create closeness on their own. Closeness usually comes from warmth, curiosity, remembering details, asking follow-up questions, sharing a little about yourself, and giving people room instead of pushing for a certain status.
    </point>
    <point>
      With the girl from class: treat that as a finished casual connection unless she starts re-engaging. One follow-up after the quarter is fine. Repeated attempts after silence are not. The lesson is not “I did everything wrong,” but “friendly weekly contact in a class context does not necessarily continue after the context ends.”
    </point>
    <point>
      Watch your internal language. “Orbiter,” “ostracized,” and comparisons with other awkward people will make you approach friendships as a grievance. Replace that with a simpler question: “Is this person reciprocating?” If yes, invest. If no, step back without turning it into a verdict on your worth.
    </point>
    <point>
      A practical filter:
      <subpoint>Do they ever initiate contact?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they ask you questions back?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they accept or suggest plans?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do they include you outside the original context?</subpoint>
      <subpoint>Do you feel more relaxed after interacting, rather than confused and scorekeeping?</subpoint>
      If most answers are no, keep it casual and move on.
    </point>
    <point>
      Your goal should not be “convert acquaintances into friends.” Your goal should be “find the people who naturally reciprocate and invest there.” That shift will make you less intense, more accurate, and more likely to actually form the friendships you want.
    </point>
  </advice>
</response>

response:
Aim less at “hiding emotions” and more at “regulating your visible stress enough to stay effective.” That matters because trying to fully conceal what you feel often backfires: people can experience it as stiffness, guardedness, or inauthenticity.

Use practical regulation techniques instead of a mask:

  <point>Slow your breathing before and during the interaction. Exhale longer than you inhale.</point>
  <point>Relax the high-tension areas that show stress first: jaw, forehead, shoulders, and hands.</point>
  <point>Speak a little slower than feels natural when nervous. Rushing is often a bigger giveaway than blushing.</point>
  <point>Pause before answering. A brief pause reads as thoughtful, not weak.</point>
  <point>Keep your face neutral-friendly rather than blank: soft eyes, unclenched mouth, slight natural smile when appropriate.</point>
  <point>Anchor attention outward onto the conversation, not inward onto “How do I look right now?” Self-monitoring tends to increase visible anxiety.</point>

For blushing specifically, the most useful trick is usually to stop fighting it. Struggling to hide it often intensifies it. If needed, briefly acknowledge nerves in a low-key way in higher-stakes settings, such as: “Let me think for a second,” or “I’m a bit keyed up, but here’s how I’d approach it.” That often comes across better than forced composure.

For interviews, prioritize these:
  <point>Prepare opening answers until they feel automatic.</point>
  <point>Do a 30-second reset before entering: breathe, drop shoulders, unclench jaw.</point>
  <point>Keep water nearby if possible and slow your first sentence.</point>

For social meetings, don’t optimize for concealment. Optimize for presence. If you are somewhat nervous but still attentive, warm, and engaged, that usually lands better than trying to look unreadable.

If your blushing or visible anxiety feels intense enough that it regularly disrupts work or relationships, it may be worth addressing the anxiety itself with a therapist or coach rather than relying on concealment tactics.

response:
You should treat this as a serious relationship problem, not something small you just need to tolerate better.

A partner who regularly insults you and the things you care about is not treating you well. Love by itself is not enough to make a relationship healthy. If being with him mostly means being put down, ignored, and saddened, then the relationship is harming you.

What to do:

  <step>Look at his current behavior, not the version of him from the first three months. The person you are dating now is someone who is mean to you and dismissive of your interests.</step>
  <step>If you want one final test of the relationship, have a direct conversation once: tell him clearly that the insults, meanness, and lack of effort are unacceptable, and that this relationship cannot continue like this.</step>
  <step>Do not argue about whether you are "too sensitive." Keep it concrete: he insults you, insults your interests, and barely spends time with you. Those are the issues.</step>
  <step>If he denies it, mocks you, blames you, or makes vague promises without real change, end the relationship.</step>
  <step>If you already feel done, you do not need to give extra chances. You can break up now.</step>
  <step>Afterward, lean on friends, family, or anyone supportive, because people in hurtful relationships often second-guess themselves once they leave.</step>

A useful question is: if nothing changed and he kept treating you exactly like this for the next year, would you want to stay? If the answer is no, that tells you a lot.

The practical advice is: either set a firm boundary immediately and require real change, or leave. Based on what you wrote, leaving is the stronger option.

  <advice>Your real issue is not the socks or the blanket. It is that you interpreted the gifts as "low effort" and then used your own $600 gift as the comparison point. That is the part you need to correct first.   <advice>You also did not give especially clear guidance. "Money so we can save" and "anime movies" is not the same as saying, "I would really like a gift card to this food place, this movie, and here is the kind of stuff I actually enjoy." If someone asks what you want and you give a broad answer, you increase the chance of a miss.</advice>
  <advice>Talk to her directly and keep it about expectations, not accusations. Say something like: "I realized I felt disappointed on Christmas, and I think part of it is that I had different expectations around gifts. I don't want to make this about money, but I want to understand how you approached my gift and talk about how we should handle holidays in the future." That gives her room to explain instead of forcing her into defense.</advice>
  <advice>When you talk, ask concrete questions: Did she have a budget limit? Did she think basics like shirts and socks were useful gifts you wanted? Did she misunderstand "money so we can save"? Was she short on time, money, or ideas? You may still dislike the outcome, but you need that information before deciding what it means.</advice>
  <advice>If this gift exchange is part of a bigger pattern—little effort, poor listening, one-sided giving, you feeling consistently overlooked—then focus on that pattern, not Christmas by itself. A pattern can justify rethinking the relationship. One bad holiday usually does not.</advice>

response:
You probably cannot lawfully keep money that was paid after your employment ended if it was a payroll mistake. The practical move is to stop spending it, keep it separate, and notify the former employer in writing as soon as possible so there is a clear record.

What to do now:
  <steps>
    <step>Do not spend the money. Leave it untouched in case they demand repayment.</step>
    <step>Contact payroll or HR in writing and state that you were terminated in January but are still receiving weekly wage payments.</step>
    <step>Ask them to stop future payments and explain how they want to handle repayment of any net amount actually received.</step>
    <step>Keep records of every payment, bank statement, and all messages you send and receive.</step>
    <step>Do not assume the money is yours just because they have not noticed yet.</step>
  </steps>

Be careful about taxes: if they reverse or correct these payments, your pay records and tax reporting may change. If the amount is large, repayment terms are disputed, or they ask for more than you actually received, talk to an employment lawyer or accountant in your jurisdiction before sending money back.

But on the core question: no safe or reliable route is apparent here for “keeping” wages that were paid after you were fired if they were not actually owed.

response:
You need to treat this less like “how do I grind harder” and more like “how do I keep this from damaging my health or collapsing in 6 weeks.”

The biggest issue is your schedule. A 7-4 and 4:30-11ish setup is not really an 80-hour plan. It is an 80-hour-plus-commuting-plus-meals-plus-getting-ready plan. In real life, that often means too little sleep, no margin for delays, and no recovery. That is what will break you first.

Here’s how to approach it:

<point>1. Protect sleep as the non-negotiable.</point>
If you are not consistently getting enough sleep, this plan is not sustainable. For most people, that means aiming for around 7.5-8 hours in bed, not “I’ll catch up later.” If your actual schedule only leaves room for 5-6 hours once commute and winding down are included, stop there: the plan is bad as designed.

Do the math honestly:
- wake-up time
- commute both ways
- shower/get ready
- meals
- time to fall asleep

If that math does not leave enough sleep, do not try to “tough it out.” Change the jobs, reduce hours, or shorten the timeline.

<point>2. Build a hard exit rule before you start.</point>
Don’t wait until you’re wrecked to decide whether it’s too much. Set objective stop conditions now, such as:
- averaging under 6.5 hours of sleep for 2 weeks
- being late more than once because of the schedule
- making repeated mistakes at work
- feeling yourself getting irritable, hopeless, numb, or reckless
- relying on heavy caffeine just to function
- falling asleep while driving or nearly doing so

If any of those happen, you adjust immediately. No “just one more month.”

<point>3. Give yourself buffer between jobs if at all possible.</point>
Your current gap is tiny. Even an extra 30-60 minutes can matter a lot. If either employer can shift your schedule a bit, try. Back-to-back full-time shifts with no margin is one of the most fragile parts of your plan.

<point>4. Keep the timeline flexible.</point>

response:
You get better at small talk the same way you get better at anything social: by lowering the stakes, using a simple structure, and practicing often.

<steps>
  <step>
    <title>Stop treating small talk like a test</title>
    <advice>Small talk is not supposed to be deep, impressive, or perfectly smooth. Its job is to create comfort and find possible connection. If you aim for “interesting,” you’ll freeze. Aim for “easy to continue.”</advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Use a basic conversation formula</title>
    <advice>Keep it simple:
      <formula>Notice → ask → listen → add a little → ask again</formula>
      <example>
        “How do you know everyone here?”
        “Oh, through work.”
        “What kind of work do you do?”
        “I’m in design.”
        “Nice. What kind of design?”
      </example>
      You do not need brilliant lines. You need follow-up questions.
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Ask questions that are easy to answer</title>
    <advice>Good small-talk questions are specific but not invasive:
      <examples>
        <item>“How’s your week going?”</item>
        <item>“What brought you here?”</item>
        <item>“How do you know the host?”</item>
        <item>“Have you been busy lately?”</item>
        <item>“What do you usually do for fun?”</item>
      </examples>
      Avoid making people do too much work with vague questions like “Tell me about yourself.”
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Use the last thing they said</title>
    <advice>If you don’t know what to say next, grab one word or topic from their last sentence and ask about that.
      <example>
        If they say, “I just got back from Chicago for a conference,” you can ask:
        <items>
          <item>“How was Chicago?”</item>
          <item>“What was the conference about?”</item>
          <item>“Do you travel for work a lot?”</item>
        </items>
      </example>
      This makes you sound engaged even if you’re nervous.
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Don’t only interview people</title>
    <advice>If you only ask questions, the conversation can feel one-sided. After they answer, add a small piece of yourself.
      <example>
        “I’ve never been to Chicago, but I’ve heard the food is great.”
      </example>
      Keep it brief, then hand it back:
      <example>
        “What was the best part?”
      </example>
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Prepare a few go-to topics</title>
    <advice>Have 5 safe topics ready:
      <items>
        <item>work or school</item>
        <item>weekend plans</item>
        <item>movies, shows, music, books</item>
        <item>food, coffee, restaurants</item>
        <item>travel, hobbies, pets</item>
      </items>
      Also prepare a few answers about yourself so you’re not caught off guard.
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Practice short conversations, not long ones</title>
    <advice>Your goal is not to become amazing at talking for an hour. Your goal is to get comfortable doing 2–5 minute conversations. That is enough to build social skill and confidence.</advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Use everyday low-pressure reps</title>
    <advice>Practice with cashiers, coworkers, classmates, baristas, neighbors. Even tiny exchanges help:
      <examples>
        <item>“Has it been busy today?”</item>
        <item>“Any plans for the weekend?”</item>
        <item>“I like your shirt—where’d you get it?”</item>
      </examples>
      Repetition matters more than intensity.
    </advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Expect some awkwardness</title>
    <advice>Good conversationalists are not people who never feel awkward. They are people who keep going anyway. A pause, a weird answer, or a missed joke does not mean you failed. It means you’re having a normal human interaction.</advice>
  </step>

  <step>
    <title>Focus on curiosity, not performance</title>
    <advice>If your attention is on “How am I coming across?” you’ll tighten up. Shift it to “What can I learn about this person?” Curiosity makes you more relaxed and more interesting.</advice>
  </step>
</steps>

<practice_plan>
  <day1>Start one brief conversation and ask two follow-up questions.</day1>
  <day2>Talk to someone and share one small thing about yourself.</day2>
  <day3>Use one prepared topic if there’s a pause.</day3>
  <day4>Practice with a low-stakes person like a cashier or coworker.</day4>
  <day5>After a conversation, write down what kept it going.</day5>
</practice_plan>

<script>
  <starter_lines>
    <item>“How’s your day been?”</item>
    <item>“What have you been up to lately?”</item>
    <item>“How do you know everyone here?”</item>
    <item>“What do you usually do when you’re not working?”</item>
  </starter_lines>
  <followups>
    <item>“How did you get into that?”</item>
    <item>“What’s that like?”</item>
    <item>“Do you enjoy it?”</item>
    <item>“What got you interested in that?”</item>
  </followups>
</script>

If you want, I can also give you a very practical small-talk cheat sheet or help you practice with example conversations.

  <advice>In most casual conversation, correcting someone mid-story that they already told you is more awkward than the repetition itself. It can make them feel embarrassed or scolded for something minor.</advice>

  </advice>

  <advice>If someone repeats themselves constantly and it’s becoming disruptive, then it’s reasonable to mention it more directly, but still kindly:
    <example>"I think I remember you telling me this before — unless there’s a new update?"</example>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You should stop trying to help her get over her ex faster.</advice>
  <advice>The right move is to respect exactly what she asked for: time.</advice>
  <advice>That means:
    <item>do not try to replace her ex emotionally</item>
    <item>do not position yourself as the solution to her pain</item>
    <item>do not keep raising the question of when she will be ready</item>
    <item>do not make big "I'd do anything for you" gestures that increase pressure</item>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you want to be helpful, be low-pressure and straightforward. You can say something like: "I care about you, and I respect that you need time. I am not going to push. If you want company or support as a friend, I'm here."</advice>
  <advice>Then follow through. Give her space. Let her initiate deeper emotional conversations about the breakup or about the two of you.</advice>
  <advice>If she reaches out, be supportive without steering everything toward romance. Listen. Keep boundaries clear. Do not treat every interaction as progress toward dating.</advice>
  <advice>You also need to accept the possibility that "give me time" may end in "I am not ready" or "I do not want this." Respecting her means allowing for that outcome, not waiting in a way that silently pressures her to choose you.</advice>
  <advice>If waiting is painful, set your own boundary. You can step back rather than hovering around in hope. That is healthier than trying to manage her healing so it matches your feelings.</advice>
  <advice>The best way to show care here is patience, emotional restraint, and respect for her pace.</advice>

response:
You need to stop treating this like a problem he is supposed to infer from hints. Have one direct conversation outside the bedroom, not right before sex, not during oral, and not right after a bad experience.

Be very specific. Say something like: “I don’t want sex to start with ‘suck it’ every time. I need kissing, touching, and foreplay that actually turns me on. I do not want you trying to just stick it in before I’m ready. If sex keeps being focused on getting you off first and then ending, I’m not going to want to keep having sex like this.”

Then tell him what you do want. Not vague criticism — concrete directions:
- “Start by kissing me.”
- “Touch me here and here.”
- “Ask me what I want.”
- “Do not ask for oral first every time.”
- “Do not try to put it in until I say I’m ready.”
- “I want sex to include my pleasure too, not just yours.”

Also set a boundary, not just a complaint. For example:
- “If you start with ‘suck it’ again, I’m going to say no and stop.”
- “If you ignore what I said and try to rush into penetration, sex is over.”
- “I’m not continuing sexual stuff that is one-sided.”

That is not punishment. It is a boundary around what kind of sex you will participate in.

His response matters as much as the sex itself. If he listens, asks questions, and tries to change, there is something to work with. If he jokes, gets mad, sulks, screams, or retreats to his game instead of engaging, then the issue is bigger than sexual technique. It means he may not be willing to take your needs seriously.

Sex by itself does not have to be a deal breaker. But a repeated pattern of selfishness, dismissal, and anger when you speak up can absolutely become one. The real question is not “should sex be a deal breaker.” The question is: “Do I want to stay with someone who keeps ignoring my clearly stated needs?”

So your next step is:
1. Have one calm, explicit conversation.
2. State what you want and what you will no longer go along with.
3. Watch what he does after that.

If nothing changes after clear communication, believe the pattern. At that point, staying and hoping he becomes considerate on his own will probably just make you more resentful.

    <point>Do not treat his virginity, by itself, as a red flag. A red flag is about harmful behavior, dishonesty, coercion, volatility, or incompatibility you can actually observe. From what you described, you have not seen that.</point>

    <point>Proceed the same way you would with anyone else: evaluate whether you enjoy his company, whether he communicates well, whether your values match, whether attraction is growing, and whether he respects boundaries.</point>
    <point>The practical difference is mainly experience level, not partner value. If things become more physical, assume you may need more explicit communication, patience, and reassurance than with someone more experienced. That is not bad; it just means you should talk clearly about comfort, consent, pace, expectations, and what each of you likes.</point>
    <point>Pay attention to how he handles being inexperienced. Good signs are honesty, willingness to communicate, ability to laugh off awkwardness, respect for your boundaries, and openness to learning. Bad signs would be entitlement, shame taken out on you, dishonesty, pressure, or rigid ideas about sex and relationships.</point>
    <point>If you are personally uncomfortable being someone’s first, be honest with yourself about that. It is okay if that is not for you. But if you continue, do it because you like him and want to get to know him, not while quietly holding his inexperience against him.</point>
    <point>If the topic comes up again, a better approach is something like: “Thanks for telling me. It doesn’t bother me. We can just go at a pace that feels good for both of us.” That acknowledges his honesty without making him feel abnormal or under review.</point>
    <point>So the answer is: keep dating him if you like him, slow down if you need to, communicate clearly, and judge him by how he treats you now—not by the fact that he had no prior dating or sexual experience.</point>

    <point>Do not treat his virginity, by itself, as a red flag. A red flag is about harmful behavior, dishonesty, coercion, volatility, or incompatibility you can actually observe. From what you described, you have not seen that.</point>
    <point>Do not interrogate him about “why” he has been celibate as if there must be a hidden problem. If he wants to share more, let that happen naturally. You can be open and curious without making him defend his past.</point>
    <point>Proceed the same way you would with anyone else: evaluate whether you enjoy his company, whether he communicates well, whether your values match, whether attraction is growing, and whether he respects boundaries.</point>
    <point>The practical difference is mainly experience level, not partner value. If things become more physical, assume you may need more explicit communication, patience, and reassurance than with someone more experienced. That is not bad; it just means you should talk clearly about comfort, consent, pace, expectations, and what each of you likes.</point>
    <point>Pay attention to how he handles being inexperienced. Good signs are honesty, willingness to communicate, ability to laugh off awkwardness, respect for your boundaries, and openness to learning. Bad signs would be entitlement, shame taken out on you, dishonesty, pressure, or rigid ideas about sex and relationships.</point>
    <point>If you are personally uncomfortable being someone’s first, be honest with yourself about that. It is okay if that is not for you. But if you continue, do it because you like him and want to get to know him, not while quietly holding his inexperience against him.</point>
    <point>If the topic comes up again, a better approach is something like: “Thanks for telling me. It doesn’t bother me. We can just go at a pace that feels good for both of us.” That acknowledges his honesty without making him feel abnormal or under review.</point>
    <point>So the answer is: keep dating him if you like him, slow down if you need to, communicate clearly, and judge him by how he treats you now—not by the fact that he had no prior dating or sexual experience.</point>
  </advice>

response:
<advice>You do not mainly need to "overcome" these feelings by yourself. You need to treat them as information. Feeling like a supporting character usually means some combination of these is happening: your labor is invisible, your life is too organized around someone else's momentum, old resentment has not been repaired, or you have stopped investing in your own identity.</advice>
  <advice>Start by separating the issues instead of blending them into one painful story.</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>Issue 1: unresolved resentment about the financial damage.</point>
    <point>Issue 2: division of roles, where you carry "boring responsibilities" and he gets novelty, movement, and recognition.</point>
    <point>Issue 3: your own sense of purpose, visibility, and authorship in your life.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>If you keep all three fused together, everything will feel like proof that you matter less.</advice>
  <advice>The next step is a direct conversation with your spouse that is not framed as "you are the main character," but as "our current structure is making me feel erased." Use specific examples.</advice>
  <advice>
    <example>"I feel like I carry the maintenance of our life while you get more growth, travel, and outward-facing opportunities."</example>
    <example>"I am still carrying hurt from the financial consequences we went through, and I don't think I've fully processed that with you."</example>
    <example>"I don't want to resent you, but I need us to look honestly at how responsibilities, freedom, and recognition are distributed."</example>
  </advice>
  <advice>Do not make the conversation only about your feelings in the abstract. Ask for structural changes.</advice>
  <advice>
    <point>A fairer redistribution of routine responsibilities.</point>
    <point>Protected time and resources for your own goals, hobbies, career development, friendships, or travel.</point>
    <point>A concrete financial recovery plan you both own, so the burden is not just emotional residue you carry alone.</point>
    <point>More acknowledgment from him of what you do to keep life functioning.</point>
  </advice>
  <advice>You should also examine whether you have been overidentifying with competence and responsibility. Sometimes the person who "handles everything" becomes indispensable but invisible. If that is happening, stop automatically absorbing all the boring labor. Let the marriage reflect two adults, not one operator and one free-moving lead.</advice>
  <advice>Then work on your own authorship. Ask yourself, apart from being a spouse, what plotline is actually yours right now? If that question feels hard to answer, that is important. Pick something concrete that belongs to you and has movement: a class, a certification, a creative project, a fitness goal, a trip, a professional shift, deeper community, something with your name on it.</advice>
  <advice>Not because self-improvement cures relationship imbalance, but because building a life you can feel inside of reduces the sense that you only exist in support mode.</advice>
  <advice>If the resentment about finances and roles is longstanding, couples counseling would likely help. Not because your marriage is doomed, but because this kind of "I disappeared into the infrastructure of our life" problem is hard to solve with one talk. It usually requires naming invisible labor, grief, fairness, and identity more carefully.</advice>
  <advice>The key shift is this: stop treating your sadness as a personal flaw to get over, and start treating it as a signal that something in the marriage and in your own life needs to be rebalanced.</advice>

response:
You should make an exit plan now, not force yourself to “get used to” a job that is already causing physical injury, exhaustion, and a sharp decline in your mental health.

Do not stay just to avoid disappointing your fiancé. This is your body and your mind, and the facts you gave are serious: 13+ hour days, heavy labor you said you could not do, bruises and scratches, no recovery time, and worsening depression. That is not a normal adjustment problem. It is a sign the job is a bad fit and may be unsafe for you.

What you should do next:
<steps>
  <step>If you can financially manage it, resign very soon—ideally with brief, professional notice if you can tolerate even that. If you truly cannot safely do another shift, it is reasonable to stop sooner.</step>
  <step>Before quitting, tell your fiancé directly that this is not about laziness or giving up; the job is physically and mentally harming you, and you already tried addressing it with the manager.</step>
  <step>Keep your explanation simple with the company: the role is not compatible with your physical limits and the schedule is not sustainable for you.</step>
  <step>Do not keep missing shifts for interviews if you can avoid it. From this point forward, either request time off, schedule around work, or leave the job and focus on your search. That is the main part of your conduct here that could fairly draw criticism.</step>
  <step>Follow up on the other job, and keep applying elsewhere immediately, especially for office or lighter-duty roles that actually match what you said you wanted.</step>
  <step>If your depression is becoming intense or you feel unsafe, treat that as urgent and reach out to a mental health professional, crisis line, or trusted person right away.</step>
</steps>

One more important point: the manager’s response about not “taking it easy” on you because you are female misses the real issue. This is not about special treatment. It is about whether the job’s physical demands and hours are compatible with your stated limitations and whether management is assigning work safely and reasonably.

So the answer is: do not “stick it out longer” just because others want you to. Leave in the most responsible way you realistically can, but leave.
